title: Troubleshooting
text:
Errors and what to do about them starts from an exception. This page starts from what you see. Each section lists the usual causes, most likely first, and links the page with the details.

Every lookup misses

The registry handed you a NullCache. A Caches lookup returns one when the cache can’t open, and while it’s disabled. Check caches[name].enabled (False on a NullCache) and caches.stats()[name].error, and look for the could not open cache line at ERROR on the diskcache_oxide logger.
A decorator bound a NullCache at import. @caches['x'].memoize() looks the cache up once, when the module is imported, and keeps what it got. If the cache couldn’t open then, the function runs uncached until a restart. Use the memoized(name) helper.
The values are there but this process can’t read them. A value of a registered type reads as a miss in a process that hasn’t registered that type, when the cache has on_decode_error='miss' (the default under durable=True), with a warning naming the tag. Register your types in a module every entry point imports: the web app, the worker, scripts.
The workers aren’t opening the same directory. A relative path resolves against each process’s working directory, which differs between a web server, a worker and a cron job. Use absolute paths.
The cache moved after a format change. A release that changed the on-disk format opens its own cache in diskcache-oxide-format-N and starts empty, with a WARNING saying so. It warms up again. See Upgrading across a format change.
Time isn’t what the cache thinks. In tests, patching time.time doesn’t move the cache’s clock; pass clock=. See Testing.
The entries really are gone. A size_limit too small for the working set evicts entries soon after they’re written. Compare volume() with size_limit, and the hit rate from stats().



The disk keeps growing

The write-ahead log. Each cache has a -wal file beside its database, trimmed back to wal_size_limit / 2 when it resets. After a burst of writes it can be much larger than the database until checkpoint() runs. See Storage and WAL.
Eviction is off. A cache with eviction_policy='none' (the recommended setting for sessions, claims and queues) holds what you put in until it expires, past size_limit if need be. Give those entries an expire, and run expire() from a scheduled job so expired ones free their space.
Expired entries that nobody removed. Expired entries are invisible to reads at once, but their space comes back only when expire() or a later write’s cleanup removes them. On a cache that’s mostly read, run expire() (or caches.expire_all()) hourly.
An old format’s cache. After a format change the old cache stays on disk beside the new one until you run remove_old_formats().
Every cache adds up. A volume holds the sum of the size_limits, about one write-ahead log per cache, and the unbounded state caches. A FanoutCache has a log per shard. Docker and Compose has the arithmetic.
Files no entry names. A crash at the wrong moment can leave a large value’s file behind. check(fix=True) removes value files no entry names once they’re an hour old.



Writes are slow under load

Many processes writing one cache. A cache has one write lock; reads never wait for it, writes queue for it. If one cache that many processes write (counters, rate limits) shows Timeout warnings or slow writes, make it a FanoutCache, which gives each shard its own lock.
A big maintenance call. clear(), expire() or cull() on a large cache takes the write lock in chunks and steps aside between them, but a write can still wait behind one. Run maintenance from one scheduled job, with its own timeout=.
A transaction held too long. Everything inside with cache.transact(): holds the write lock. Keep transactions short and do slow work outside them. See Transactions.
A slow disk. A cache on a slow, emulated or network filesystem writes and checkpoints slowly, and on a network filesystem it isn’t safe at all: keep it on a local disk.



PermissionError

Another user created the directory. Cache directories are created owner-only (0700), so only the user that created one can open it. A script run with sudo, a root cron job, or a docker exec -u root that touched the directory first leaves it owned by root. Fix the ownership (chown -R), and run everything that shares a cache as one user. See Open a cache.
A container with a different UID. Every container that shares a volume must run as the same user, and that user must never change between image versions. See Docker and Compose.
Windows: the files are open. Windows won’t delete a file a process has open, so removing a cache directory while a handle is open fails. close() every handle first. See Windows.



Which format is this cache in?
cache.directory ends in diskcache-oxide-format-N when the cache was opened in a versioned subdirectory after a format change; otherwise it’s the directory you passed, in this release’s format. To read a database’s format without opening it as a cache, use the standard library’s sqlite3, read-only, from a separate process (a shell or a script), never from one that has the cache open: closing a second SQLite library’s connection to the same file can drop the locks the cache holds on it.
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect('file:/var/lib/my-app/cache/pages/diskcache-oxide.sqlite?mode=ro', uri=True)
print(con.execute('PRAGMA user_version').fetchone()[0])  # 3 for 0.2.3 and later
con.close()


Still stuck
Run cache.check(): it reports damage to the database, value files that don’t match their entries, and totals that don’t add up. If it looks like a bug in diskcache-oxide, see If it looks like a bug.

title: Switching from python-diskcache
text:
If you’re here, the question is a practical one: what breaks? Very little, and on purpose. diskcache-oxide is API compatible with python-diskcache 5.6.3’s Cache and FanoutCache, and it is not data compatible. Keeping diskcache’s API makes switching a one-line change. Leaving its on-disk format behind is what made it possible to fix the design underneath, pickle included. So the switch itself is small, and the rest of this page is about what you’ll notice afterwards: mostly fixes, and now and then something stricter.
diskcache is also unmaintained. Its last release, 5.6.3, came out in August 2023, the repository has had no commits since 2023, and its open issues and pull requests go unanswered. The bugs this page mentions were found by running diskcache-oxide’s test suite against it, and each one has a standalone reproduction in the repository’s upstream/ folder.
For most apps, switching looks like this:

title: Switching from python-diskcache
text:
State that isn’t cache
A cold start costs a cache nothing but speed. Some of what apps keep in diskcache isn’t cache, though: sessions, queued jobs, counters, a Deque or Index. Deal with those before you switch. Drain a queue with the old code first, and flush counters. See State that isn’t really cache, which applies here too. For entries you must keep, copy them across once, with every writer stopped:
import time

import diskcache
from diskcache_oxide import Cache

MISSING = object()
old = diskcache.Cache('/var/cache/my-app')
new = Cache('/var/lib/my-app/state/sessions', eviction_policy='none')

for key in old.iterkeys():
    value, expire_time, tag = old.get(key, default=MISSING, expire_time=True, tag=True)
    if value is MISSING:
        continue  # expired, or deleted while copying
    expire = None if expire_time is None else expire_time - time.time()
    if expire is not None and expire <= 0:
        continue
    try:
        new.set(key, value, expire=expire, tag=tag)
    except TypeError as exc:  # a key or value diskcache-oxide can't store without pickle
        print(f'skipped {key!r}: {exc}')
Keys and values go through diskcache-oxide’s rules: a key that isn’t a key type, or a value of a class you haven’t registered, raises TypeError and is skipped. Register your types before the loop, or open the new cache with pickle=True if it really holds arbitrary objects. A Deque or Index has no equivalent yet: copy its items into a work queue or plain keys.

title: Switching from python-diskcache
text:
Upgrading diskcache-oxide
During 0.x, a release that changes the on-disk format bumps the minor version and says so first in its changelog entry. 0.2.3 was one: it added tags and the eviction policy, as format 3. Since 0.3.5, a release that meets a cache in another format doesn’t fail: it opens a new, empty cache in the subdirectory diskcache-oxide-format-N and logs a warning, so old and new workers each keep a working cache during a rolling deploy. Once the old workers are gone, remove_old_formats() removes the old cache. A release that keeps the format keeps your caches warm. The details, including what to do about queues and sessions first, are in Upgrading across a format change.

title: Switching from python-diskcache
text:
Settings passed as keywords
diskcache takes its settings as keyword arguments (Cache(directory, statistics=1)). diskcache-oxide’s constructors list theirs explicitly, so a diskcache-only keyword raises TypeError: unexpected keyword argument. Here’s where each went:

size_limit, cull_limit: the same, persisted in the cache (size_limit at least 1 MiB)
eviction_policy: the same name; 'least-recently-stored' or 'none'
sqlite_cache_size: the same name, in 4 KiB pages per connection; default 256 (1 MiB), not diskcache’s 8192
statistics: gone; call cache.stats(enable=True), which counts per process, in memory (D-049)
tag_index: gone; tags are always indexed
disk_min_file_size: gone; values of 64 KiB or more always go to files
disk_pickle_protocol: gone; no pickle by default; pickle=True uses the highest protocol
sqlite_journal_mode: gone; always WAL, checked at open
sqlite_synchronous: gone; always NORMAL, as diskcache’s default
sqlite_mmap_size, sqlite_auto_vacuum: gone; not configurable

New settings with no diskcache counterpart: serializer, pickle, types, clock, max_connections, wal_size_limit, wal_checkpoint, on_decode_error and durable. Cache lists them.

title: Serialization
text:
A cache has a quiet second job: it’s a program that reads bytes it didn’t write, left on disk by whatever process got there first. That makes the serializer the most security-relevant piece of the whole library, and it has three jobs. What goes into the cache should come out as exactly what you put in. Encoding and decoding should be fast, because they happen on every call. And reading the cache should never run code that someone else left there. diskcache’s default, pickle, does the first two well and fails the third by design: unpickling runs whatever the bytes tell it to. diskcache-oxide gets all three, and pickle becomes something you opt into, one cache at a time.

Two formats
Each cache picks a structured format with serializer=:
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')                       # msgpack, the default
readable = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-json', serializer='json')

msgpack (the default) is compact and fast. On a 450 KB page-cache entry it’s about 25× faster than tagged JSON, and it stores nested bytes without base64.
json is human-readable: open diskcache-oxide.sqlite in any SQLite browser and read your values. It uses serde_json with exact float round-tripping. Keys aren’t JSON: str keys show as text, and keys of other types as a short binary encoding (see Keys and tags).

Plain str and bytes values skip both and are stored raw. Every row records how it was encoded, so if you change a cache’s serializer, existing entries stay readable.
Everything stored as a value goes through the same encoder: what you pass to set(), add() and push(), and what a memoized function returns.


Exact types
JSON turns tuples into lists and can’t store sets, datetimes, NaN, very large ints, or dicts with non-str keys. msgpack has some of the same gaps. The usual answer is to coerce quietly and let the bug show up later.
diskcache-oxide’s encoder, written in Rust, notices anything its format would change and tags it instead, so it decodes back to the same type:

tuple: a tuple, not a list
set: a set
frozenset: a frozenset
datetime.datetime: a datetime, with its timezone and microseconds
datetime.date: a date
decimal.Decimal: a Decimal, exact
int wider than 64 bits: the same int
float('nan'), inf, -inf: the same float
bytes nested in a container: bytes
dict with int (or other non-str) keys: the same keys

import datetime

cache.set('record', {
    'created': datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC),
    'point': (37.77, -122.42),
    'ids': {101, 102},
    'big': 2**128,
    'by_id': {1: 'one', 2: 'two'},
})

record = cache.get('record')
assert isinstance(record['point'], tuple)
assert record['by_id'][1] == 'one'
User data can’t be mistaken for a tag: a dict that happens to look like one is escaped on the way in and decoded as an ordinary dict on the way out.


What isn’t stored
A value that neither format can represent exactly, such as an instance of your own class, raises TypeError at set():
cache.set('service', MyService())
# TypeError: values of type MyService can't be stored without pickle (only exact built-in types round-trip)
Only exact built-in types count. A subclass of dict or str isn’t stored as its base type, because it wouldn’t come back as the class you stored. Failing at set() time means you find out where the value was created, not three requests later when something reads it. For a type of your own, or one from a library, register it.
A memoized function that returns such a value raises the same TypeError, after the function has run, when the result is stored. Nothing is cached, so the next call runs it again and raises again. Register the type, or have the function return something storable.


Your own types
Most of what an app stores that isn’t a built-in is a type it doesn’t own: a bson ObjectId inside a session dict, a namedtuple a library hands back, the str subclass a Markdown renderer returns. Converting those by hand at every call site works, but it’s the kind of code that drifts. Instead, tell the codec once how to store the type:
from bson import ObjectId
import diskcache_oxide

diskcache_oxide.register_type(ObjectId, name='bson.ObjectId', encode=str, decode=ObjectId)

cache.set('session', {'id': ObjectId(), 'user': ObjectId()})
cache.get('session')['id']   # an ObjectId again
encode turns an instance into a value the codec can already store, built-ins or other registered types, nested as deep as you like. decode turns that value back into an instance. The registration is process-wide, so make it at import time, in every process that opens the directory.
A dataclass needs only a name. Its init=True fields are read straight off the instance, with no intermediate dict, and on the way out it’s rebuilt with cls(**fields), so defaults and __post_init__ still run:
@dataclasses.dataclass
class Episode:
    id: int
    title: str
    published: datetime.datetime | None = None

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Episode, name='tp.Episode')
cache.set('episode:491', Episode(491, 'Rust and Python'))
The write path skips dataclasses.asdict(), which deep-copies: on a 20-field dataclass a set() goes from about 23 µs to 18. A read still builds one keyword dict and calls the constructor, so it saves almost nothing (4.0 µs against 3.8), and that’s fine: a cache is mostly reads, and what you gain is the call sites.
What the registry guarantees:

Nothing is imported by name. A registered value is stored as {"$t:bson.ObjectId": "..."}, and a reader looks that name up in its own registry. A process that hasn’t registered it gets ForeignValueError, and the row stays for one that has. That is the whole difference from pickle.
The name is yours. Rename or move the class and the stored rows still read, because the tag is the name you chose, not the class’s path.
Lookup is by exact type. A subclass of a registered class is its own registration. The codec’s own types (str, dict, datetime and the rest) can’t be registered, since their wire form is a contract across versions; their subclasses can, which is how a namedtuple or a str subclass gets in.
A registered type is never pickled, even on a cache with pickle=True. Once the encoder has used a registration for any part of a value, that value is stored through it or set() raises: if its encode raises, or returns something the codec can’t store. You registered it to stay off pickle, and a silent fallback would hide the bug.
Last registration wins, by class and by name, so a module that a dev server reloads can register its new class object again.
A decode function’s errors are classified as a pickle hook’s would be. A Timeout or OSError raises with the row kept (a miss under durable=True). An error about the row, such as a TypeError from a dataclass row written before a field was removed, becomes CorruptValueError with yours as __cause__, and on_decode_error='miss' deletes that row so the writer replaces it. Decode runs while the cache holds a connection, as unpickling does, so a slow decode delays forks and checkpoints for as long as it runs; one that re-enters the cache is fine.

A cache that needs a different encoding of a type than the rest of the process gets its own registry, consulted before the global one:
reg = diskcache_oxide.TypeRegistry()
reg.register(ObjectId, name='bson.ObjectId', encode=lambda o: o.binary, decode=ObjectId)
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-binary-ids', types=reg)
Two processes with different registrations on one directory write rows the other can’t read, the same way two processes with different serializer= settings would. Register at import time, the same way everywhere.


Why pickle is off by default

Unpickling runs code. Anyone who can write to the cache directory, including a compromised neighbor process or a shared volume, can make every reader run arbitrary Python.
Pickle hides mistakes. Database sessions, open files and other objects that were never meant to be cached get pickled without complaint and fail later in confusing ways.



Opting in to pickle
When you really do need to cache arbitrary objects, turn pickle on for that cache. It’s used only for values the structured format can’t represent; everything else is still stored as msgpack or JSON.
objects = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-objects', pickle=True)
objects.set('service', MyService())
A good habit is to give pickled values their own cache directory, and keep everything else in a cache without pickle.


Reading safely: UnsafeValueError
Several processes can open one directory with different settings. A handle opened without pickle=True never unpickles. If it reads a value that a pickle=True handle stored, it raises diskcache_oxide.UnsafeValueError (a TypeError subclass) and leaves the row in place, so the pickle=True handle can still read it.
A value whose stored bytes can’t be decoded at all raises CorruptValueError (a ValueError subclass).


Keys and tags
Keys follow stricter rules than values, because a key has to be compared, sorted and found as well as read back. They never go through serializer=, pickle= or the type registry. A key can be:

str, bytes, bool or None
an int that fits in 64 bits
a float, except NaN, which raises ValueError because it isn’t equal to itself
a tuple of any of these, nested up to 32 deep

cache.set(('episode', 491, 'transcript'), text)
cache.set(b'\x9f\x02', blob)
cache.set(42, 'the answer')
Anything else raises TypeError, even on a pickle=True cache: a list, a dict, a bytearray, an object, a registered type, and subclasses such as an IntEnum, a StrEnum or a namedtuple. If your key is an enum member, use its .value; if it’s a namedtuple, pass tuple(point).
Keys compare by exact type, so 1, 1.0 and True are three different keys. Python’s == says they’re equal, and diskcache treats 1 and 1.0 as one key, so code that mixes them finds nothing where it expected a hit. The exception is -0.0, which is the same key as 0.0, as it is in a dict.
A str key is stored as plain text. Every other key is stored in a compact binary encoding that sorts the way the values do, which is why iterkeys() can walk them in order: every str key first, then None, the bools, ints, floats, bytes and tuples, each group sorted. iterkeys(prefix=...) matches str keys only, so if you plan to list or delete a group of keys by prefix, make them strings ('user:42:profile', not ('user', 42, 'profile')).
A memoized function’s key is a tuple built from its name and its arguments, so every argument it’s called with must be one of these types. A call with a list or an object raises TypeError before the function runs. Leave arguments like a database connection out of the key with ignore=.
Tags, from set(..., tag=...) and memoize(tag=...), follow the same rules as keys and are stored the same way. evict(1) removes entries tagged 1 and leaves the ones tagged 1.0 or True.

title: Performance
text:
A microsecond is nothing until you multiply it. Web apps call their cache on almost every request, often straight from the asyncio event loop, where every microsecond the cache spends is a microsecond every other request on that loop waits. So diskcache-oxide’s performance work starts with read latency, then throughput under many threads, then predictable resource use. Correctness always comes first: every speedup has to keep the conformance suite green, or it doesn’t ship. The numbers below are the ones that survived.

The numbers
Measured with bench/gate.py, which runs python-diskcache 5.6.3 (its last release, from August 2023; the project has had no commits since) and diskcache-oxide in the same session on the same machine, in four interleaved rounds. These numbers come from an 18-core Apple M5 Max on macOS 27.2, on AC power with nothing else heavy running, measuring the 0.3.5 code on 2026-11-13 (bench/results/macos/gate-3.14.txt and gate-3.14t.txt in the repository). Both libraries ran in the same session, so the ratios compare like with like; the absolute numbers on an x86-64 Linux server will differ. Latencies are p50 in microseconds. Ratios are oxide’s time divided by diskcache’s, so lower is better.









Workload
3.14
3.14t (free-threaded)




get, small value, hit
0.90 µs (0.49×)
0.88 µs (0.54×)


get, miss
0.76 µs (0.54×)
0.76 µs (0.57×)


get, small dict
1.32 µs (0.52×)
1.36 µs (0.57×)


get, random keys over a large database
2.64 µs (0.79×)
2.68 µs (0.85×)


set, small value
18.5 µs (0.75×)
18.3 µs (0.76×)




Threaded throughput, every thread sharing one Cache, in operations per second at 1/2/4/8 threads (ratios are oxide’s throughput over diskcache’s, so higher is better):









Mix
3.14
3.14t (free-threaded)




99:1 reads to writes
687k / 682k / 675k / 670k (1.6-34.8×)
690k / 766k / 951k / 753k (1.5-2.1×)


1,000:1 reads to writes
770k / 762k / 758k / 758k (1.7-39.7×)
777k / 1,054k / 1,294k / 915k (1.5-2.5×)




Two things stand out:

On GIL builds, diskcache collapses as threads are added and oxide doesn’t. At 99:1, diskcache drops from about 419k to 19k operations per second going from 1 to 8 threads; oxide stays flat around 670-690k. diskcache’s per-thread connections end up fighting over the GIL and SQLite’s locks.
On free-threaded builds, oxide is faster at every thread count, but it doesn’t scale yet. At 1,000:1 throughput peaks at about 1.3M operations per second at 4 threads, 1.7× one thread, and falls back to about 0.9M at 8. That’s what the free-threaded work below is for.

Run them yourself with python -m bench.gate. Numbers vary by machine; the ratios are what the gate enforces.


Where the speed comes from

Rust from the call to the disk. A get goes from Python straight into compiled Rust: one prepared SQLite statement, decode, done. There’s no Python wrapper in between.
Statements prepared once. Each pooled connection caches its prepared statements, so a lookup never recompiles SQL.
The clock is read in Rust. Checking expiry doesn’t call back into Python’s time.time().
Fast codecs. msgpack and tagged JSON are encoded and decoded in Rust, building Python objects directly.
Reads never write. Least-recently-stored eviction means a get never updates anything, so any number of readers proceed in parallel.
A smarter write lock. Writers in one process queue on an in-process lock per database file, instead of every thread retrying against SQLite’s busy handler.
SQLite tuned for it. The bundled SQLite is built with its global memory statistics turned off, which removes a process-wide mutex from every allocation: 2-10% more threaded throughput.



Prefix scans at scale
diskcache’s iterkeys() gets slower faster than the cache grows: about 1.7 seconds at 100,000 keys, and over 25 seconds at 400,000. diskcache-oxide’s iterkeys(prefix=...) is an indexed range scan, paged in batches so no read transaction is held between them. 400,000 keys scan in about 10 ms.


Memory that stays flat
Memory is bounded by configuration, not by how many threads touch the cache: at most max_connections connections per database file (default 8), each with a 1 MiB page cache. A FanoutCache defaults to two per shard for the whole root, about 16 MiB at 8 shards. A separate memory-instrumented build runs bench/memory.py and the memory tests under heavy load to hold that bound. See Storage and WAL.


Known slow spots
Two oversubscribed cases measure slower than before the SQLite mutex spin and the connection-slot spin went in. Both are known, and neither is in the path of a web app running a few threads per process.

A plain Cache with far more threads than cores, all sharing one handle: 7% slower on an M-series Mac at 36 threads, and 5% in a Linux VM at 32. Faster hand-off lets more threads into SQLite at once.
A FanoutCache at max_connections=32 with 8 threads, on macOS only: 5-12% slower. The same case on Linux is 41-56% faster.



Next: free-threaded scaling
Profiling a cached get shows that about 60% of its time is one system call: SQLite taking its shared-memory read lock on the -shm file, under a process-wide mutex. It’s the biggest single cost on every read, and it’s also what keeps free-threaded throughput from scaling. The free-threaded phase on the roadmap, after the Django backend, goes after it, along with:

a per-process lock-caching layer under SQLite, or longer-lived read snapshots;
thread-affine connections;
cheaper reference counting on shared Cache objects in free-threaded builds;
making threads that share one handle scale. FanoutCache is built and removes the multi-process write-lock ceiling, but at its default settings it doesn’t lift this read ceiling, so the shared per-handle path is being worked on.

Past that, the network server can go further still: as the only owner of its files, it can use SQLite’s exclusive locking mode, which keeps that lock in ordinary memory. Measured reads drop from 1.18 µs to 0.69 µs.

title: New to caching? Start here
text:
If you’ve never put a cache in front of anything, this page is the ten minutes that make the rest of the docs read easily. If you have, skip to Getting started; nothing here is specific to diskcache-oxide except the examples.

What a cache is
A cache is a copy of an answer, kept somewhere cheaper to reach than wherever the answer came from. The database can tell you the ten most popular episodes, but it takes a few milliseconds and some of its attention to do it, and the answer is the same for everyone who asks in the next five minutes. So you ask once, keep the answer, and hand out the copy.
Something is worth caching when all three of these are true:

It’s asked for repeatedly. An answer nobody asks for twice is a copy nobody reads.
It costs something to produce. A database query, a call to another service, rendering a page, a calculation. A cache lookup costs about a microsecond in diskcache-oxide, so anything slower than that is a candidate, and anything that takes milliseconds is a good one.
A slightly old answer is acceptable, or you can tell when it stops being right. This is the one that bites, and the rest of this page is mostly about it.

Here it is in the smallest possible form. The first call does the work; the second gets the copy:

import tempfile
import time

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())

def popular_episodes() -> list[str]:
    episodes = cache.get('episodes:popular')          # a hit returns the copy
    if episodes is None:                               # a miss: nothing cached, or it expired
        time.sleep(0.05)                               # stands in for the database query
        episodes = ['Rust for Python developers', 'Free-threaded Python', 'SQLite everywhere']
        cache.set('episodes:popular', episodes, expire=300)
    return episodes

for attempt in ('first call', 'second call'):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    popular_episodes()
    print(f'{attempt}: {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.2f} ms')

first call: 59.95 ms
second call: 0.02 ms


That shape, check the cache, do the work on a miss, store the result, is called cache-aside, and it’s the one you’ll use most. @cache.memoize() wraps it up as a decorator; the caching recipe shows how.


Why bother
Three reasons, and you usually get all three at once:

Latency. The page that took 300 ms takes 3, because the slow parts were answers you already had.
Load. The database answers a question once a minute instead of once a request. That’s the difference between a database that’s fine and one you’re upgrading at 2 a.m.
Protection. When the thing behind the cache is slow, flaky or rate-limited (a partner API, a search service), the cache keeps serving the last good answer while it recovers.

The flip side: a cache is a copy, and copies go out of date. Every design decision in caching is a trade between how fresh the answer is and how cheap it is to serve.


The words

Hit / miss: A lookup found a live entry, or didn’t. The hit rate is the fraction of lookups that hit; a cache with a low hit rate is costing you writes for nothing.
Key: The name an entry is stored under. In diskcache-oxide a key is usually a string like user:42:profile; numbers, bytes and tuples such as ('user', 42) work too.
Expiry (TTL): How long an entry stays valid. After it, a lookup misses as if the entry were gone. expire=300 means five minutes.
Stale: Still cached, but no longer what the source would say. Expiry bounds how stale an entry can get.
Invalidation: Removing or replacing an entry because its source changed, instead of waiting for it to expire.
Eviction: The cache removing entries to stay under its size limit. diskcache-oxide evicts the least recently stored entries first, or nothing at all under eviction_policy='none'. Eviction is why a cache can never be the only copy of something you need.
Cold / warm: A cold cache is empty (just deployed, just cleared) and every lookup misses until it’s warm. The first minutes after a deploy are the slow ones.
Stampede (thundering herd): A popular entry expires and every worker recomputes it at the same instant. See Serving stale values while refreshing.
Negative caching: Caching “there’s no such thing” so a missing record doesn’t cost a database query every time someone asks. Use a short expiry.



The first hard thing: invalidation

There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.
Phil Karlton

(The popular extension adds “and off-by-one errors”, which is funnier if you don’t count.)
Invalidation is hard because the cache can’t know when the source changed. It has a copy of the answer; it has no idea the user just renamed themselves. Something has to tell it, and the three ways to do that are the whole of the art:

Let it expire. Give every entry an expire, chosen by how stale you can stand: five minutes for a popular list, an hour for a rendered page, a day for a thumbnail. It’s the simplest strategy, it needs no knowledge of where the data changes, and it’s the one safety net that catches every mistake in the other two. Always set an expiry, even when you also invalidate explicitly. An invalidation you forgot is otherwise forever.
Invalidate at the write. When your code saves the user’s new name, it also deletes user:42:profile. The next read misses and rebuilds. This gives exact freshness, at the cost of knowing every key the change affects, which is where naming (below) comes in. When many keys depend on one thing, delete them by prefix, store them with a shared tag and drop them all with evict(tag), or change a generation number so the old keys are never read again: Invalidating groups of keys.
Put the version in the key. If the key is episode:512:v7:page, then publishing revision 8 means readers ask for episode:512:v8:page, miss, and rebuild, and the old entry is simply never asked for again. Nothing is deleted; the stale copy expires on its own.

Most apps use all three: an expiry on everything, a delete where the write is obvious, and versioned keys for things that have a natural version. Here’s the expiry half, with a fake clock so it runs instantly:

now = [1_000_000.0]
cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=lambda: now[0])

cache.set('user:42:profile', {'name': 'Sam'}, expire=600)
print('right away:   ', cache.get('user:42:profile'))

now[0] += 601                                          # ten minutes pass
print('after expiry: ', cache.get('user:42:profile'))

cache.set('user:42:profile', {'name': 'Sam'}, expire=600)
cache.delete('user:42:profile')                        # the user renamed themselves: invalidate at the write
print('after delete: ', cache.get('user:42:profile'))

right away:    {'name': 'Sam'}
after expiry:  None
after delete:  None


One more rule that saves real grief: never cache a value that depends on who’s asking under a key that doesn’t say who’s asking. A profile page cached as page:profile will be shown to the next user who asks for it. If the answer depends on the user, the locale, the plan, or the A/B group, the key includes them.


The second hard thing: naming
Keys are names, and the two problems turn out to be the same problem: an invalidation can only find the entries whose names tell it what they depend on. Some conventions that hold up:

General to specific, separated by colons: user:42:profile, episode:512:transcript. Everything about user 42 then shares the prefix user:42:, and a prefix scan (iterkeys(prefix='user:42:')) finds all of it in time proportional to how many there are, not the size of the cache.
End a prefix with the separator. user:4 also matches user:42; user:4: doesn’t.
Include everything the value depends on, and nothing it doesn’t. A key with the request’s timestamp in it never hits. A key without the locale serves French pages to English readers.
Keys are cheap. A long, descriptive key costs almost nothing; a short, clever one costs you a debugging session later.



What goes wrong, and the fix

Stale data. Shorter expiry, or an invalidation at the write. If you can’t say which writes affect an entry, the expiry is your answer.
A stampede after a deploy or an expiry. Refresh hot entries ahead of time, or serve the stale copy while one worker rebuilds: Serving stale values while refreshing.
Cached errors. Don’t cache the result of a failed call as if it were an answer. Cache “not found” briefly if you must; never cache a 500.
Treating the cache as storage. An entry can be evicted or expire at any moment, and a deploy can clear the whole directory. Anything you can’t rebuild from somewhere else (a session, a one-time token, a counter you haven’t flushed) belongs in a cache of its own, opened with eviction_policy='none' so nothing is evicted for size, and ideally also somewhere permanent. The sessions and counters recipes show the pattern.
A bug that might be the cache. Turn caching off without touching the code that uses it, with NullCache, and see whether the bug survives.



Where diskcache-oxide fits
There are three usual places to keep a cache, and the choice is about who can see it and what survives:










A dict in the process
diskcache-oxide
A cache server (Redis)




Shared across worker processes
No, one copy per worker
Yes, every process on the machine
Yes, every machine


Survives a restart
No
Yes, it’s a directory
Depends on configuration


Cost of a lookup
Nanoseconds
About a microsecond
A network round trip


Something extra to run
No
No
Yes, a server



The in-process dict is unbeatable for a single process and useless the moment you have four gunicorn workers. The server is the right answer when the cache has to be shared across machines. diskcache-oxide is the middle: a cache that’s just a directory, shared by every thread and process on the machine, still there after a restart, and fast enough that you stop thinking about the lookup. Because every process sees the same directory, it also covers a few jobs people often run Redis for on a single machine: locks and rate limits, counters and work queues. Getting started is the next page.

title: FanoutCache: sharded caches
text: A plain Cache has one write lock per database file, which makes it a shop with one checkout lane: readers walk straight through, but every writer queues, and eight worker processes that all bump counters are eight carts in one lane. A FanoutCache opens more lanes. It’s one cache spread over several SQLite databases, called shards. Each key lives in exactly one shard, chosen by a fixed hash of the key, so writes to different keys go to different files and stop queueing on one lock. It has the same methods as Cache for single keys, and it’s one directory, shared by any number of threads and processes.

title: FanoutCache: sharded caches
section: Plain Cache and FanoutCache directories don’t mix
text:
Plain Cache and FanoutCache directories don’t mix
A Cache opened on a FanoutCache’s directory, or on one of its shard directories, raises LayoutMismatchError, and so does a FanoutCache opened on a plain Cache’s directory. The refused open creates nothing, so a typo doesn’t leave a directory that neither kind can open. LayoutMismatchError is both a ValueError and a FormatMismatchError. If a registry hits it, the lookup returns a NullCache and reports it like any failed open. That holds for a shard directory in any on-disk format.
A root in another on-disk format, whether its manifest or any of its shards, opens as a whole in the root’s diskcache-oxide-format-N subdirectory, a new root with its own shards and the count you ask for (or 8), and logs a warning, as a plain Cache does. One shard never moves on its own. remove_old_formats() removes the old root’s shards, highest first, and its manifest last. See Upgrading across a format change. A registry that meets another shard count than its registration’s opens the folder with the count on disk and warns instead (Caches).

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
diskcache-oxide’s test suite is a conformance suite: the same black-box tests run against real diskcache 5.6.3 and against diskcache-oxide. Where they behave differently, it’s on purpose, and it’s written down here. Running one suite against two implementations turned out to be a bug detector pointed in both directions: most of the differences below are diskcache bugs the suite found, each with a reproduction in the repository’s upstream/ folder.
A divergence is never a way to skip a failing test. The full record, including test names and measurements, is tests/DIVERGENCES.md.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-001: no pickle by default
diskcache pickles every value. diskcache-oxide stores str and bytes raw and everything else as msgpack or tagged JSON. A value the format can’t represent exactly raises TypeError at set() unless the cache was opened with pickle=True. A cache opened without it never unpickles: reading a pickled value written by a pickle=True peer raises UnsafeValueError and leaves the row alone. Unpickling runs code from whatever is in the cache directory, and silently pickling hides values that were never meant to be cached. See Serialization.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-015: owner-only directories
A cache directory diskcache-oxide creates, and its value-file subdirectories, are 0700. Existing directories are never changed. Anyone who can write to a cache directory can poison the cache, and its contents (keys with IP addresses in them, for example) can be private.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-021: directory is required
diskcache creates a temporary directory if you don’t give one. A cache directory is shared state and a security boundary, and an implicit temp directory is almost never what a multi-process app wants.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-008: NaN round-trips
In diskcache, set('k', float('nan')) succeeds but get('k') returns None, ignoring any default. In diskcache-oxide it’s a float like any other.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-010: expire() removes everything that has expired
text:
D-010: expire() removes everything that has expired
diskcache’s expire() works in chunks of 100, and when expired entries share one expiry time it stops after the first chunk. With 250 such entries, one call removes 100. diskcache-oxide removes all of them, still in chunks so writers can get in between.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-011: clear() keeps concurrent writes
diskcache’s clear() keeps deleting until the cache is empty, including entries written while it runs. In a reproduction with 50,000 entries and a concurrent writer, it deleted 76,000 writes that had already succeeded, and its running time grew with the write rate. diskcache-oxide’s clear() removes only entries that existed when it started, and always finishes. evict(tag) is bounded the same way.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-013 and D-016: large values under pressure
text:
D-013 and D-016: large values under pressure
If a large value’s file disappears, diskcache returns the default but the key still reads as present in in and len. diskcache-oxide treats it as a miss and removes the orphaned row.
When one process overwrites a large value while others read it, diskcache occasionally returns the default for a key that was never deleted, which makes callers recompute a hot value for nothing. diskcache-oxide’s readers detect the overwrite and retry, so they always get a whole value, old or new.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-014: no booleans for numbers
bool is an int subclass, so in diskcache expire=True is a one-second TTL and expire=False stores an already-expired entry. diskcache-oxide raises TypeError: a bool there is almost always an argument in the wrong position.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-012: forks while another thread writes
text:
D-012: forks while another thread writes
When a process forks while another of its threads is in a write transaction, diskcache’s child inherits a lock nobody in the child will release, and its first write stalls for the full timeout (60 seconds by default). Under a busy read/write load that hits 20-50% of forks. diskcache-oxide’s fork barrier waits for in-flight transactions before the fork, so the child can always write. See Concurrency and forks.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-020: forking inside your own transaction
text:
D-020: forking inside your own transaction
CPython won’t let a library stop a fork, and a transaction held by the forking thread itself can’t be waited for. In diskcache the child stalls behind it. In diskcache-oxide, the child’s copy of the transaction is poisoned and its writes to that database raise RuntimeError immediately, and the parent gets a RuntimeWarning.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-029: tx is the cache, and every handle shares it
text:
D-029: tx is the cache, and every handle shares it
diskcache’s with cache.transact() as tx: binds tx to None, and a second Cache on the same directory has its own connection, so its transact() inside the first one’s block waits for the write lock until it times out. In diskcache-oxide tx is the cache itself, and on the thread that entered the block every call on that directory runs in the transaction, through any handle: a transact() on a second handle joins the outer one instead of waiting. Other threads’ calls never join it. See Transactions.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-030: TransactionBusy, and what retry=True retries
text:
D-030: TransactionBusy, and what retry=True retries
Inside one cache’s transaction, diskcache’s transact() on a second cache waits for its write lock until it times out, and retry=True loops on any sqlite3.OperationalError. When another thread holds that lock, diskcache-oxide raises TransactionBusy, a Timeout subclass, at once: that thread could be waiting for a lock this one holds, and no timeout setting fixes that. retry=True retries a plain Timeout and never TransactionBusy, and checks for Ctrl-C between attempts.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-031: a transaction can end on another thread
text:
D-031: a transaction can end on another thread
diskcache says a transaction “may not be shared between threads”. In diskcache-oxide any thread may commit or roll back the owner’s transaction through its __exit__, within the transaction’s timeout. A commit that can’t run in time raises Timeout and rolls back, and the owner’s own exit afterwards raises TransactionAborted (a RuntimeError) unless the transaction committed, so a with block never exits cleanly when its writes are gone. An owner’s exit during another thread’s commit waits for the outcome.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-017 and D-018: bounded connections
diskcache opens a connection for every thread that uses a cache, so 64 threads hold 131 files open in the cache directory, and close() closes only the calling thread’s connection. diskcache-oxide uses a pool per database file, at most max_connections (default 8), and the last close() closes every connection, so the directory is safe to move or delete afterwards.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-019: opening never writes
Opening an existing diskcache commits a write transaction even when nothing changed. diskcache-oxide’s open, and reads after it, never write, so a read-mostly worker or a read-only copy of the directory never takes the write lock.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-023: bounded SQLite memory
diskcache’s default is a 32 MiB page cache and a 64 MiB memory map per connection, with one connection per thread. diskcache-oxide’s sqlite_cache_size defaults to 256 pages (1 MiB) per pooled connection, so SQLite’s memory per directory stays around 8 MiB per process.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-024: a WAL that shrinks
With readers in other processes, a burst of writes makes SQLite’s write-ahead log grow to fit the burst and stay that size: hundreds of MiB to over 1 GiB beside a database of a few MiB. diskcache-oxide trims the log whenever it resets (wal_size_limit), offers checkpoint() to empty it on demand, checkpoints a large log at close(), and can checkpoint automatically with wal_checkpoint='auto', which tries a few times in a row so that a reader in flight in another process doesn’t defeat it. See Storage and WAL.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
FanoutCache (D-032 to D-040)
These are covered together in FanoutCache: sharded caches, and listed against diskcache’s in Switching from python-diskcache.

D-032: the shard count is part of where every key lives, so it’s recorded, and a different shards= never changes it: the cache opens with the stored count and logs a warning, or raises LayoutMismatchError with raise_on_mismatch=True, instead of quietly losing data and atomicity.
D-033: the hash is fixed by its definition and part of the format, and iterkeys(prefix=) gives FanoutCache the ordered listing Cache has.
D-034: a silently dropped write and a hang are both worse than an error the caller chose how to handle; durable=True is that choice.
D-035: a maintenance job must finish in bounded time, and when it can’t, it must say what it did.
D-036 and D-037: budgets (size, connections, file descriptors) follow configuration, not the number of threads or shards.
D-038: a typo shouldn’t leave a directory that neither kind of cache can open, or a shard written behind the FanoutCache’s back.
D-039: shards is keyword-only so that the second positional argument is timeout, as on Cache. The sub-collections and read() would each need their own design across shards, so they aren’t copied from diskcache (see the roadmap). Everything else on Cache, apart from the queue calls, works on a FanoutCache too.
D-040: holding every shard’s lock would serialize the whole cache behind one transaction, which is what sharding exists to avoid.

title: Concurrency and forks
text: A production Python web app is a crowd. Several worker processes, often several threads in each, a pre-forking server that creates and recycles those workers while they’re busy, and a cron job or an admin script opening the same cache on the side. More and more, it’s also free-threaded Python, where the threads really do run at the same time. diskcache-oxide is designed for all of that at once, and its test suite runs each of these cases on every change, because this is where cache bugs hide: not in get and set, but in what happens when two of them collide.

title: Concurrency and forks
text:
A bounded connection pool
diskcache opens a SQLite connection for every thread that touches the cache and keeps it. With 64 threads that’s 131 open files in the cache directory, and a server with enough threads runs out of file descriptors.
diskcache-oxide shares a pool of connections per database file across every handle in the process:
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', max_connections=8)   # the default
The pool never holds more than max_connections connections, so at most 2 × max_connections + 1 files are open in the cache directory, however many threads you run. A thread that finds every connection busy waits for one, up to the cache’s timeout. When the last handle on a directory closes, every connection closes with it, whichever threads used them.

title: Concurrency and forks
section: How long a call waits for a fork
text:
How long a call waits for a fork
A fork counts against timeout. A cache call behind a pending fork waits for it through the call’s own timeout and then raises Timeout, so timeout has to exceed the work in flight, plus the fork, plus the interpreter hand-off. A fork takes about a millisecond in a quiet small process, but tens to hundreds of milliseconds beside busy threads on a GIL build (the forking thread has to get the interpreter back), longer in a large process, and it waits for work in flight such as a forced checkpoint. A timeout under that sees Timeout during ordinary forks, and a loop on timeout=0 adds to the problem by being one of those busy threads.
A fork waits for every transaction another thread holds, with no timeout of its own, so a long transaction delays every fork in the process. Code that holds a transaction or runs inside a pickle hook (or a registered type’s decode function, which runs in the same place), and waits for another thread’s cache call, can keep a fork from finishing: the fork waits for that code, and the other thread waits for the fork. That other thread’s call now raises Timeout, and the fork finishes once your code lets go. Until it does, os.fork() doesn’t return, a second os.fork() queues behind it, and every thread with no transaction or hook of its own gets Timeout on every Cache in the process, after using up its whole timeout (60 seconds by default). Other processes aren’t affected. If the code never reacts (a hook that retries forever, or one blocked on something that isn’t a cache call), the fork stays stuck. A hook stuck in C code that holds the GIL stops everything, as it would without a cache.
Two calls don’t raise. checkpoint() returns False when a fork keeps it from running. close() takes at most about 2 seconds behind a stuck fork, 1 for the checkpoint and 1 for the release, and del about 1, whatever timeout is. An ordinary fork ends well inside that, so close() waits it out as usual. If the fork outlasts it, close() returns anyway and the connections close when the fork ends.
Before-fork hooks run in reverse registration order, and logging and concurrent.futures each take a lock in theirs and keep it until the fork is over. diskcache_oxide makes sure its own hook runs before those two, so they stay usable while a fork waits for your code: a pickle hook or a decode function can still log or submit work. Two things it can’t fix. Another library’s hook that takes a lock and is registered after diskcache_oxide stays held while a fork is stuck. And a thread that calls the cache while holding logging’s module lock can hold up a fork until that call’s timeout.
With durable=True, a Timeout behind a fork is a miss or False rather than an exception on a single-key call, so a timeout shorter than this makes ordinary forks into misses. A pickle hook or a registered type’s decode that re-raises the Timeout it got from another thread’s call lets go of its level under any policy, which clears the stuck fork. What durable=True adds is that the request doesn’t fail: that Timeout is a miss, with the row kept.

title: Concurrency and forks
section: Forking from inside your own transaction
text:
Forking from inside your own transaction
CPython won’t let a library refuse a fork, so the barrier can’t wait for a transaction held by the very thread that is forking. The child’s copy of that transaction is poisoned: anything done inside it raises RuntimeError and nothing commits, and the child’s writes to that database raise RuntimeError straight away instead of stalling for a minute. A transact() in the child doesn’t join the inherited transaction either: it raises RuntimeError too. The parent’s block carries on and commits as usual, and the parent gets a RuntimeWarning. A clear error at the call site beats a mysterious 60-second hang in a fresh worker.

# diskcache-oxide

A cache that is a directory: every thread and process that opens the same path shares one cache, and it survives restarts. It keeps python-diskcache's `Cache` API and rebuilds the engine in Rust on SQLite: reads in under a microsecond, writes atomic across processes, safe across `fork()`, no pickle unless asked for, bounded memory and disk. Measured against python-diskcache 5.6.3 (unmaintained: no commits since 2023) on the same machine: a cached `get` in 0.90 µs at p50 (0.49× diskcache's), and at 8 threads sharing one `Cache` about 670,000 operations a second where diskcache falls to 19,000; eight writing processes on a `FanoutCache` reach about 1.5 million a second. It is not data compatible with diskcache (it uses `diskcache-oxide.sqlite`, never `cache.db`). Errors an agent will meet: `TypeError` at `set()` for a value the formats can't represent, `Timeout` (a `TimeoutError`) when a lock stays busy, `UnsafeValueError` when a `pickle=False` cache reads a pickled row, `FormatMismatchError` only where a format change can't be handled (another format inside a `diskcache-oxide-format-N` subdirectory, or 0.2.3 and earlier meeting a newer cache), and `LayoutMismatchError` when a directory holds the other kind of cache. A cache directory holding another on-disk format isn't an error since 0.3.5: the cache opens in its versioned subdirectory with a warning.

## Install

Install with `pip install diskcache-oxide` (CPython 3.14 or 3.15, GIL or free-threaded; wheels for macOS arm64, Linux x86_64/aarch64 and Windows x86_64, elsewhere a source build that needs the latest stable Rust). The import is `diskcache_oxide`. During 0.x a release that changes the on-disk format bumps the minor version. Since 0.3.5, a cache directory holding another format (older or newer) doesn't fail to open: the cache opens in the subdirectory `diskcache-oxide-format-N` (N = this release's format, 3 since 0.2.3), logs a `WARNING` on the `diskcache_oxide` logger once per process, and every later open uses that subdirectory; `directory` reports it. A `FanoutCache` moves as a whole. `cache.remove_old_formats()` (and `caches.remove_old_formats()`) removes caches in an older format from the directory, only files diskcache-oxide wrote, and returns what it removed; it does not check whether an old worker still runs, so call it only after every older worker has stopped (on Linux and macOS, a still-running old worker's cache can be corrupted). 0.2.3 and earlier still raise `FormatMismatchError` on a newer format, and 0.2.3 doesn't know the subdirectory: after a cleanup it creates its own format-3 cache at the root, which is safe but not shared with newer workers.

## Use

```python
from diskcache_oxide import Cache, Timeout

# Open once per process and share it across threads; every worker opens the same path.
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', timeout=1.0)

cache.set('episodes:popular', episodes, expire=300)  # always give cached values an expire
episodes = cache.get('episodes:popular')  # None (or default=) on a miss

# Atomic across processes: exactly one caller gets True.
if cache.add('job:refresh', os.getpid(), expire=3600):
    refresh()

try:
    cache.set(key, value, expire=60)
except Timeout:  # the write lock stayed busy for `timeout`: skip the cache, never fail the request
    pass
```

An app with several caches registers them once and looks them up by name; a cache that can't open comes back as a `NullCache` and is retried after 10 s. The recommended production setup: a durable registry for rebuildable data, and state (sessions, job claims, locks, queues) as plain caches opened directly, never through the registry (a `NullCache`'s `add()` always wins and its `push()` stores nothing) and never durable, under one directory the app owns:

```python
caches = Caches('/var/lib/my-app/cache', durable=True, timeout=1.0)
caches.register('pages', size_limit=2 * 2**30)
caches['pages'].get('/about')

coordination = Cache('/var/lib/my-app/state/coordination', timeout=3.0, eviction_policy='none')
coordination.add('job:nightly', 1, expire=3600)  # exactly one worker wins
```

Plain caches, not `FanoutCache`, unless many processes write one cache at once.

In tests: `Cache(tmp_path / 'cache')` per test, `NullCache()` where caching must not interfere, and `Cache(tmp_path, clock=fake_clock)` to test expiry without sleeping. If tests patch `time.time`, pass `clock=lambda: time.time()`, since the cache reads the clock natively.

## Rules

- Keys are `str`, `bytes`, `int` (64-bit), `float`, `bool`, `None`, or tuples of those, never pickled; a `list`, `dict`, object, subclass (`IntEnum`, `namedtuple`) or int past 64 bits is `TypeError`, a NaN `ValueError`. They compare by exact type: `1`, `1.0` and `True` are three keys. For a prefix scan use `str` keys with a trailing separator (`user:42:` so `user:4` doesn't match `user:42`): `prefix=` sees only `str` keys.
- Values are exact built-ins only: `str`, `bytes`, `int`, `float`, `Decimal`, `bool`, `None`, and `list`, `tuple`, `dict`, `set`, `frozenset`, `datetime` and `date` made of those, all round-tripped exactly (tuples stay tuples, big ints and NaN survive). A dataclass, ORM row or `dict` subclass raises `TypeError` at `set()`. Register the type instead: `diskcache_oxide.register_type(Episode, name='app.Episode')` for a dataclass (fields stored, rebuilt with `Episode(**fields)`), or `register_type(ObjectId, name='bson.ObjectId', encode=str, decode=ObjectId)` for anything else, at import time in every process. The name is the tag on disk; a reader without the registration gets `ForeignValueError` and the row stays. A registered type is never pickled. If arbitrary objects are really needed, give them their own `Cache(dir, pickle=True)`.
- A `pickle=False` cache never unpickles: reading a row a `pickle=True` handle wrote raises `UnsafeValueError` (a `TypeError`) and keeps the row. This is a configuration mistake, not damage, so it raises under every `on_decode_error` and `durable` setting.
- `bool(cache)` means "caching is on" (`Cache` and `FanoutCache` are always truthy, `NullCache` is falsy). Never use `if cache:` for "is it empty"; use `len(cache)`.
- `Timeout` subclasses `TimeoutError`. The default `timeout` is 60 s; in a request path use `timeout=1.0` and treat `Timeout` as "don't cache this time". A fork counts against `timeout`, and a fork hand-off can take tens to hundreds of milliseconds, so keep about a second in a pre-forking server.
- `expire=True` and `timeout=True` raise `TypeError` (a bool there is an argument in the wrong position). `size_limit` under 1 MiB raises `ValueError`. `directory` is required.
- Open a cache once per process and share it across threads. The same directory opened twice in one process shares one connection pool. Use `with Cache(...) as cache:` or call `close()`; a closed handle reopens on its next use. Forks need nothing from you: a fork barrier waits for other threads' writes and the child opens fresh connections.
- `add()` is the claim primitive: one winner across processes. A `NullCache.add()` always returns True and a `durable=True` `add()` returns False on an outage, so keep job claims and locks on a plain handle in their own small directory, with an `expire`.
- `incr()`/`decr()` are atomic across processes and keep the entry's existing expiry; `incr()` on a missing key starts from `default` (0) and creates an entry that never expires. For a windowed counter, `add(key, 0, expire=2 * window)` then `incr(key)`. `default=None` makes a missing key a `KeyError`.
- `iterkeys(prefix=...)` is an indexed range scan in sorted order, safe to delete from while iterating. Without a prefix it lists `str` keys first, then `None`, bools, ints, floats, bytes and tuples, each sorted. `iter(cache)` is insertion order. An entry leaves `get`, `in`, `len()` and iteration the moment it expires (D-060); its row and space stay, in `volume()`, until a `set()` sweeps a few or `expire()` removes them, so schedule `expire()` hourly on a mostly-read cache.
- `with cache.transact() as tx:` groups writes on the calling thread; `tx` is the cache itself. Commit on exit, roll back on an exception, a nested block joins the outer one, a block whose writes were lost raises `TransactionAborted` (a `RuntimeError`) at exit. Never `await` inside the block. Beginning a transaction on a second cache whose lock another thread holds raises `TransactionBusy` at once, and `retry=True` retries only `Timeout`. On a `FanoutCache`, `transact(key=k)` locks one shard, and inside it any call for a key on another shard, or over every shard (`len`, `volume`, iteration, `clear`, `expire`, `cull`, `checkpoint`), raises `ValueError`; a bare `transact()` there is a `TypeError`.
- `durable=True` is "the cache can't take a request down", not database durability. On an outage a single-key call returns its miss value (`get` the default, `set` False, `incr` `default + delta`) and logs once a minute on the `diskcache_oxide` logger. It can drop writes, so a dropped `set` or `delete` serves stale data until the entry expires. `timeout` bounds waiting for a lock or a fork, not disk work: on a saturated disk a commit can still take seconds. The constructor, admin calls (`clear`, `expire`, `cull`, `checkpoint`, `len`, `volume`, iteration), transactions and bugs (`TypeError`, `UnsafeValueError`) still raise. Pair it with a small `timeout`.
- `on_decode_error='miss'` (the default under `durable=True`) makes a value that can't be decoded a miss: the row is deleted and a warning logged. A row a newer version or another host might read (`ForeignValueError`) is a miss that keeps the row. A function in its place is called as `report(key, exc)`; from a `Caches` registry it is `report(name, key, exc)`.
- `NullCache(invalidate=real)` forwards only removals (`delete`, `pop`, `clear`, `evict`, `iterkeys`) to the real cache. An overwriting `set` or a version-bump `incr` is dropped while caching is off, so invalidate by deleting. The queue calls are never forwarded. A `NullCache` never encodes values, so it accepts a value a real cache refuses with `TypeError`: don't test value types only against a `NullCache`.
- On a `NullCache`, `push()` returns a key and stores nothing (the job is lost), `pull()`/`peek()` return the default, a memoized function runs every call, and `get(k, tag=True)` is `(default, None)`. Keep queues, claims and locks on a cache that's never switched off.
- `Caches`: register every cache at startup, before handing any out. `caches[name]` reads a plain cache and `caches.fanout(name)` one registered with `shards=` (the other way is a `TypeError`). Passing `shards=` at all, even `shards=None`, registers a `FanoutCache`. A registered `shards=n` applies only to a new folder: an existing folder keeps its own count, and the registry logs a WARNING (and one ERROR per process) instead of failing; to change the count, delete the folder with every worker stopped. `disable()`/`enable()` change later lookups only. `@caches[name].memoize()` binds at import to whatever the lookup returned (a `NullCache` if the open failed, forever); look the cache up per call if that matters. Registry `stats()` gives `CacheStats` (count, volume); hit/miss counts are `caches[name].stats()`. Locks, claims, sessions and queues are plain `Cache(...)`s opened directly, never registered: a registry hands out a `NullCache` when one can't open.
- `FanoutCache` is for several processes that write often. `shards` is keyword-only (`FanoutCache(path, 4)` is `timeout=4`), the count is recorded and permanent for the directory (a different `shards=` keeps the stored count with a `WARNING`, or raises `LayoutMismatchError` with `raise_on_mismatch=True`), a plain `Cache` and a `FanoutCache` refuse each other's directories, `max_connections` and `size_limit` are totals (at least `shards` connections and `shards` MiB). It does not make threads sharing one handle faster.
- Cache directories must be on a local disk. SQLite's WAL mode is required: an open where SQLite declines WAL (some FUSE mounts) raises `RuntimeError` naming the journal mode, but NFS, SMB, EFS and Azure Files usually accept WAL and then corrupt, which can't be detected, so never use them (or a Kubernetes ReadWriteMany volume). New directories are created `0700`. A directory is a cache or a parent of caches, never both: never nest a cache inside another cache's directory.
- After a big fill or `clear()`, call `cache.checkpoint()` so the write-ahead log is truncated; `close()` does it for a large log; `wal_checkpoint='auto'` is the opt-in for long-running writers. Put maintenance (`expire()`, `checkpoint()`) in one scheduled job, not in every worker.
- `@cache.memoize(name=None, typed=False, expire=None, tag=None, ignore=())` caches a function's results, with diskcache's key shape (`f.__cache_key__(*args, **kwargs)` gives it, for `cache.delete(...)`). Call it with parentheses. `ignore` is the fifth positional argument (after `tag`), so pass it by name. Every argument not in `ignore` must be a key type, or the call raises before the function runs; put connections and clients in `ignore`. `expire=0` never stores; `None` results are cached; `async def` is refused. On a `NullCache` it runs every call.
- `retry=True` (keyword-only) on `get`, `set`, `add`, `delete`, `pop`, `touch`, `incr`, `decr`, `expire`, `cull`, `clear`, `evict` and the queue calls keeps retrying a `Timeout` until it gets through, even under `durable=True`. Use it for background jobs, not request paths. `cache[k]` never retries. `transact(retry=True)` sleeps between attempts.
- Coordination: `Lock(cache, key, expire=...)`, `RLock`, `BoundedSemaphore(cache, key, value=n)`, `Averager`, `@throttle(cache, count, seconds)`, `@barrier(cache, Lock)` and `@memoize_stampede(cache, expire)`, from `diskcache_oxide`, atomic across processes. Use a small cache of their own (culling and `clear()` remove lock keys); give a `Lock` an `expire`. They raise `TypeError` on a `NullCache` or `durable=True` cache (`memoize_stampede` doesn't), and `RuntimeError` if they'd wait inside a `transact()` on their own cache.
- `stats(enable=True, reset=False) -> (hits, misses)` counts `get` and `cache[k]` per process, in memory, never in the database; counting is off until the first `stats()` call turns it on. `check(fix=False, retry=False)` returns a list of `warnings.WarningMessage`; `fix=True` removes broken entries and old orphan files, then `VACUUM`s (slow on a big cache, needs temp space, blocks writers and forks). `reset('size_limit' | 'cull_limit' | 'eviction_policy', value)` persists a setting for every process, and without `value` reads the stored one. `reversed(cache)`, `pop(key, expire_time=True)`, and pickling a cache (it reopens the directory) work.
- Tags: `set(k, v, tag='user:42')` (`tag=` is keyword-only, any key type, compared by exact type), `get(k, tag=True)` returns `(value, tag)`, and `evict('user:42')` removes every entry that had that tag when it started; an overwrite without `tag=` clears the tag, while `touch`, `incr` and `add` on a live key keep it. `memoize(tag=...)` tags every stored result. `1`, `1.0` and `True` are three tags. `eviction_policy='none'` (keyword-only, stored in the cache) never evicts for size: use it for locks, claims and anything that must not vanish, and give those entries an `expire`. `'least-recently-used'` and `'least-frequently-used'` raise `ValueError`.
- Queues (`Cache` only, not `FanoutCache`): `push(value, prefix=None, side='back', expire=None, *, tag=None, retry=False)` returns the key; `pull(prefix=None, default=(None, None), side='front', *, expire_time=False, tag=False, retry=False)` returns `(key, value)`, or `(None, None)` when empty, and each item goes to exactly one caller; `peek(...)` the same without removing; `peekitem(last=True, ...)` the newest or oldest entry, `KeyError` when empty. Open a queue's cache with `eviction_policy='none'` (least-recently-stored would evict the queue's front) and use a prefix no other key starts with. `side` must be `'front'` or `'back'` (`ValueError`).
- Not available yet, so don't generate calls to them: `Deque`, `Index`, `AsyncCache`, `FanoutCache.cache()`/`deque()`/`index()`, and `read()`/`read=`. LRU/LFU eviction and `disk=` aren't coming.

## Decision table

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| One process, or mostly reads | `Cache(directory)` |
| Several worker processes that write often (counters, rate limits, claims) | `FanoutCache(directory, shards=8)` |
| Many caches in one app, an admin page, switching one off by name | `Caches(base_dir, timeout=1.0, ...)` then `register(name, ...)` |
| Caching off in tests, local dev or while chasing a stale-data bug | `NullCache()`, or `NullCache(invalidate=real)` so deletes still land |
| A cache outage must cost speed, never a request | `Cache(..., timeout=1.0, durable=True)` |
| A value that can't be decoded should be a miss, not an exception | `on_decode_error='miss'` or `on_decode_error=report` |
| Store a dataclass, an `ObjectId`, a namedtuple, a `str` subclass | `register_type(cls, name=..., encode=..., decode=...)`; a dataclass needs only `name=` |
| Cache arbitrary objects | register the type; otherwise a separate `Cache(dir, pickle=True)` |
| Inspect rows by hand in a SQLite browser | `serializer='json'` |
| Several writes that must land together | `with cache.transact() as tx:`; on a `FanoutCache`, `transact(key=k)` |
| Exactly one worker runs a scheduled job | `cache.add('job:x', os.getpid(), expire=interval - margin)` on a plain, never-null handle |
| Per-client rate limit shared by every worker | `add(f'rate:{client}:{window_no}', 0, expire=2 * window)` then `incr(...) <= limit` |
| Invalidate everything about one user or object | `set(..., tag='user:42')` then `evict('user:42')`; or `iterkeys(prefix='user:42:')` plus `delete`; or a generation number in the key |
| Cache a function's results | `@cache.memoize(expire=...)`; `@memoize_stampede(cache, expire)` when a recompute is expensive and many callers miss at once |
| A cross-process lock, semaphore or rate limit | `Lock`, `BoundedSemaphore`, `throttle` on a plain `Cache(dir, eviction_policy='none')`, not durable, never a `NullCache` |
| A work queue shared by worker processes | `push(value, prefix='jobs')` / `pull(prefix='jobs')` on a `Cache(dir, eviction_policy='none')` (not a `FanoutCache`) |
| Tests of expiry without sleeping; tests that patch `time.time` | `Cache(tmp_path, clock=fake)`; `clock=lambda: time.time()` |
| A huge `-wal` file after a write burst | `cache.checkpoint()`, or `Cache(..., wal_checkpoint='auto')` |
| Type a function that accepts any cache | `CacheLike`; `TransactionalCacheLike` if it calls `transact()`; `ShardedCacheLike` for `transact(key=)` |

## API

- `Cache(directory, timeout=None, *, size_limit=None, cull_limit=None, eviction_policy=None, serializer='msgpack', pickle=False, types=None, clock=None, max_connections=None, sqlite_cache_size=None, wal_size_limit=None, wal_checkpoint='manual', on_decode_error=None, durable=False)`: raises `ValueError`/`TypeError` for bad settings, `LayoutMismatchError` or `FormatMismatchError` for a directory this build can't use, `Timeout` if another process holds it locked. Defaults: `timeout` 60 s, `size_limit` 1 GiB, `cull_limit` 10, `max_connections` 8, `wal_size_limit` 64 MiB.
- `get(key, default=None, *, expire_time=False, tag=False, retry=False)`, `set(key, value, expire=None, *, tag=None, retry=False) -> bool`, `add(key, value, expire=None, *, tag=None, retry=False) -> bool`, `delete(key, *, retry=False) -> bool`, `pop(key, default=None, *, expire_time=False, tag=False, retry=False)`, `touch(key, expire=None, *, retry=False) -> bool`, `incr(key, delta=1, default=0, *, retry=False)`, `decr(...)`, `memoize(name=None, typed=False, expire=None, tag=None, ignore=())`, `iterkeys(*, prefix=None, reverse=False)`, `expire(*, timeout=None, retry=False) -> int`, `clear(*, timeout=None, retry=False) -> int`, `evict(tag, *, timeout=None, retry=False) -> int`, `cull(*, timeout=None, retry=False) -> int`, `reset(key, value=ENOVAL)`, `stats(enable=True, reset=False)`, `check(fix=False, retry=False)`, `push`, `pull`, `peek`, `peekitem`, `volume() -> int`, `checkpoint(*, timeout=None) -> bool` (False when busy, never raises for that), `close(*, checkpoint=True)`, `transact(retry=False)`; plus `cache[key]`, `cache[key] = value` (never expires), `del cache[key]`, `key in cache`, `len(cache)`, `iter(cache)`, `reversed(cache)`, `with`. Properties: `directory`, `timeout`, `size_limit`, `cull_limit`, `eviction_policy`, `enabled`, `durable`.
- `FanoutCache(directory, timeout=None, *, shards=None, ..., raise_on_mismatch=False)` (a `shards=` that differs from the root's stored count keeps the stored count and logs a `WARNING`, or raises `LayoutMismatchError` with `raise_on_mismatch=True`; a root in another format redirects either way) with the same settings, single-key methods, `memoize`, `evict`, `stats`, `check` and `reset` (a `size_limit` is split across shards), no queue calls, plus `shards`, `shard_of(key) -> int` and `transact(*, key, retry=False)`. Its `clear`/`expire`/`cull`/`checkpoint` share one `timeout` across the shards and, on failure, raise with `failed_shards` and `removed` attributes.
- `remove_old_formats() -> list[str]` on `Cache` and `FanoutCache` (`[]` on `NullCache`): removes caches in an older on-disk format from the cache's directory and returns the paths removed. No check for other processes: call it only once every older worker has stopped. `directory` is where the cache really is (the versioned subdirectory after a format change); reopen with the original directory, not `directory`.
- `NullCache(directory=None, timeout=None, *, ..., invalidate=None)`: accepts and ignores `Cache`'s settings; `get`/`pop` return the default, `set`/`add` return True, `incr` returns `default + delta`, everything else is 0, False or empty; `transact()` is a no-op yielding itself.
- `Caches(base_dir, *, on_open_error=None, retry_open_after=10.0, **defaults)`: `register(name, *, directory=None, **settings)`, `caches[name]`, `fanout(name)`, `disable(*names)`, `enable(*names)`, `enabled(name)`, `stats() -> dict[name, CacheStats]`, `clear(name, *, timeout=None)` (raises if it can't open), `expire_all(*, timeout=None)`, `remove_old_formats() -> dict[name, list[str] | None]`, `close_all()`, `with`.
- Protocols: `CacheLike`, `TransactionalCacheLike` (adds `transact(retry=False)` and `push`/`pull`/`peek`/`peekitem`), `ShardedCacheLike` (adds `transact(*, key, retry=False)`). `Cache` and `NullCache` are transactional; `FanoutCache` and `NullCache` are sharded.
- `register_type(cls, *, name, encode=None, decode=None)`, `unregister_type(cls) -> bool`, `registered_types() -> dict[str, type]`, on the process-wide `registry: TypeRegistry`; `TypeRegistry()` with the same `register`/`unregister`/`registered` for one cache's `types=`. Own built-in types can't be registered (`ValueError`); one of `encode`/`decode` alone, a non-dataclass with neither, or a dataclass with an `InitVar` is `TypeError`.
- Exceptions: `Timeout(TimeoutError)`, `TransactionBusy(Timeout)`, `TransactionAborted(RuntimeError)`, `UnsafeValueError(TypeError)`, `CorruptValueError(ValueError)`, `CorruptKeyError(CorruptValueError)` (iteration met a stored key it can't read), `ForeignValueError(CorruptValueError)`, `FormatMismatchError(RuntimeError)`, `LayoutMismatchError(FormatMismatchError, ValueError)`.
- Warnings from `check()`: `UnknownFileWarning`, `EmptyDirWarning`. Sentinels: `ENOVAL`, `UNKNOWN`. Types: `Key` (the key union), `Memoized`, `Memoizer`, `CacheStats`. Recipes: `Lock`, `RLock`, `BoundedSemaphore`, `Averager`, `throttle`, `barrier`, `memoize_stampede`.
- `sqlite_version()`, `sqlite_compile_options()`, `BUNDLED_SQLITE_VERSION`, `__version__`. Logging goes to the `diskcache_oxide` logger. There is no CLI and no environment variable to configure.

## Reading an error

```text
TypeError: values of type Episode can't be stored without pickle (only exact built-in types round-trip)
```

It is raised by `set()`, where the value was created, not by a later `get()`. Fix in this order: register the type (`register_type(Episode, name='app.Episode')`), or store a dict (a `model_dump()`), then, only if arbitrary objects are really required, open a separate `Cache(other_dir, pickle=True)` for them. A registered type that still raises has an `encode` that raised or returned something unstorable, or a field that is; that raises even with `pickle=True`. Don't add `pickle=True` to the shared cache to make the error go away: every reader of that directory then runs unpickle on whatever is written there.

```text
diskcache_oxide.Timeout: timed out after 1 s waiting for a lock or a pending fork
```

Someone held the write lock (a `clear()` in a maintenance script, a long `transact()` block, a fork in flight) for longer than `timeout`. In a request, catch it and skip the cache. If it's common, raise `timeout`, move maintenance to one scheduled job, shorten transaction blocks, or move many writing processes to a `FanoutCache`. `durable=True` turns it into a miss for single-key calls.

memoize with cache stampede protection, as diskcache’s: a result close to expiry is


Usage
Source

    cache, expire, name=None, typed=False, tag=None, beta=1, ignore=()
)


recomputed early, in a background thread, by one caller (Vattani et al., VLDB 2015), while every caller keeps getting the cached result. Results are stored as (result, seconds it took).
