title: TypeRegistry
text:
register()

Register cls under name.


Usage
Source


register(cls, *, name, encode=None, decode=None)


With encode and decode, encode(instance) must return a value the codec can already store (registered types included, nested) and decode(value) must give the instance back. With neither, cls must be a dataclass: its init=True fields are stored and read back with getattr, and it is rebuilt with cls(**fields), so defaults and __post_init__ run. A field removed or made required between the write and the read makes that row a CorruptValueError.
Lookup is by exact type: a subclass of a registered class is not registered. Last registration wins, by class and by name, so a reloaded module can register its new class object again.


Parameters


cls: type[T]

The class. Not one of the codec’s own exact types (str, int, dict, datetime, …), whose wire form is fixed; their subclasses are fine.

name: str

The tag written into every row. Yours, so a class rename never orphans stored rows.

encode: Callable[[T], object] | None = None

Instance to a storable value.

decode: Callable[[Any], T] | None = None

That value back to an instance.





Raises


 ValueError

An empty name, or one of the codec’s own types.

 TypeError

cls isn’t a class; only one of encode/decode was given; neither was given and cls isn’t a dataclass, or is one with an InitVar field (the constructor needs it but no instance holds it: pass explicit functions).

title: NullCache
text:
A switched-off cache, so app code needs no if cache is None checks.


Usage
Source


NullCache(
    directory=None,
    timeout=None,
    *,
    size_limit=None,
    cull_limit=None,
    eviction_policy=None,
    serializer="msgpack",
    pickle=False,
    types=None,
    clock=None,
    max_connections=8,
    sqlite_cache_size=None,
    wal_size_limit=None,
    wal_checkpoint="manual",
    on_decode_error=None,
    durable=False,
    invalidate=None
)


It behaves like a real cache in which every entry expires the instant it’s written and is swept straight away: reads miss, writes succeed, and it’s always empty. It’s falsy, and its enabled is False.


Parameters


directory: str | os.PathLike[str] | None = None

Accepted and ignored, like every other Cache argument, so switching between the two is a one-line change.

invalidate: CacheLike | None = None

A real cache to forward removals to (delete, pop, clear, evict and iterkeys), so invalidation by removal still lands while caching is off. Writes aren’t forwarded: an overwriting set or a version-bump incr is dropped, and the old value is served once caching is back on.

from diskcache_oxide import Cache, NullCache

cache = NullCache()
cache.set('k', 1)        # True, and nothing is stored
cache.get('k', 'miss')   # 'miss'
cache.add('job', 1)      # True: don't claim jobs on a cache that might be off

real = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')
off = NullCache(invalidate=real)
off.delete('user:42')    # removed from `real`; off.get('user:42') is still None

title: FanoutCache.transact()
text:
A write transaction on the shard key lives in, for with cache.transact(key='total') as tx:.


Usage
Source


FanoutCache.transact(*, key, retry=False)


It is Cache.transact() on that one shard: tx is this FanoutCache, calls on this thread inside the block for keys on that shard run in the transaction (through any handle on the root), it commits when the block exits and rolls back if the block raises, and a nested transact for a key on the same shard joins it. Other threads’ and processes’ writes to that shard wait for it; the other shards are not locked.
Inside the block, a call on this thread for a key on any other shard raises ValueError, reads included, through any handle on the root, and so does a transact for a key on another shard (its writes could not be in the transaction). Use shard_of to check that keys share a shard. Calls over every shard raise ValueError on this thread inside the block too: len(), volume(), iter(), iterkeys() (and next() on an iterator made before the block), clear(), expire(), cull() and checkpoint(). They would run inside the transaction on its shard and outside it on the others.
The check costs one atomic load while no transaction is open anywhere in the process; while one is (any thread’s, any cache’s), keyed calls, calls over every shard and iterator next()s also look at each shard that holds one.
As on Cache, a transaction belongs to a thread, not an asyncio task, a block that didn’t commit raises TransactionAborted at its exit, and under durable=True a failure to begin, or inside the block, raises.


Parameters


key: Key

Keyword-only. Any key on the shard to hold; it needn’t exist.

retry: bool = False

As for Cache.transact().

retry: bool = False

On a Timeout, try again until the call gets through, each round with the whole timeout, a durable=True handle included. Only Timeout is retried.





Raises


 TypeError

key isn’t a str, or retry isn’t a bool.





Examples
with cache.transact(key='totals:2026-11') as tx:
    n = tx.get('totals:2026-11', 0)
    tx.set('totals:2026-11', n + 1)

title: FanoutCache
text:
A disk cache split over several SQLite databases (shards), so reads and writes on different keys


Usage
Source


FanoutCache(
    directory,
    timeout=None,
    *,
    shards=None,
    size_limit=None,
    cull_limit=None,
    eviction_policy=None,
    serializer="msgpack",
    pickle=False,
    types=None,
    clock=None,
    max_connections=None,
    sqlite_cache_size=None,
    wal_size_limit=None,
    wal_checkpoint="manual",
    on_decode_error=None,
    durable=False,
    raise_on_mismatch=False
)


don’t queue on one file’s locks.
Each key lives in exactly one shard, chosen by a hash that is part of the on-disk format: every process, and every release, sends a key to the same shard. The root records its shard count, so every handle agrees on it. Single-key calls behave exactly as on Cache, on the key’s shard. len() and volume() add up every shard under one timeout.
clear(), expire(), cull() and checkpoint() run on every shard in turn, under one timeout for the whole call. If a shard fails, the others are still done, and then the first failure raises, as its own type (so except Timeout still works), with two extra attributes and a note naming them:

failed_shards: a tuple of the indexes of the shards that failed, in order.
removed (not on checkpoint()): how many entries the call removed in all, from every shard, including what a failed shard removed before it failed.



Parameters


directory: str | os.PathLike[str]

The root directory. It holds the manifest (diskcache-oxide-fanout) and one directory per shard, 000 to NNN. It must not be a plain Cache’s directory. If its manifest or any shard is in another on-disk format, the whole cache opens in the root’s diskcache-oxide-format-N subdirectory instead, as for Cache, never one shard alone.

timeout: float | None = None

As for Cache (default 60). Opening, len(), volume(), clear(), expire(), cull(), checkpoint() and close() share one timeout across every shard, not one each.

shards: int | None = None

How many shards, 1 to 256. None (the default) uses the count the root records, or 8 for a new root. A count that differs from the recorded one opens with the recorded count and logs a WARNING on the diskcache_oxide logger, once per process; changing the count needs a new directory. Each shard takes about 4 file descriptors to open, and 2 more per connection it opens in use, so 256 shards need over 1,024: more than Linux’s default ulimit -n. Too few raises OSError (EMFILE) with the numbers.

size_limit: int | None = None

The disk budget in bytes for the whole cache, split evenly (floored) across the shards, each of which culls on its own. Each shard needs at least 1 MiB, so the total must be at least shards MiB. With none given, a new root gets 1 GiB in all.

cull_limit: int | None = None

As for Cache, per shard.

eviction_policy: Literal["least-recently-stored", "none"] | None = None

As for Cache, on every shard.

serializer: str = "msgpack"

As for Cache.

pickle: bool = False

As for Cache.

types: TypeRegistry | None = None

As for Cache.

clock: Callable[[], float] | None = None

As for Cache.

max_connections: int | None = None

The most SQLite connections this process opens for the whole cache, split across the shards (the first max_connections % shards get one more). At least shards. The default is two per shard, and never fewer than 8 in all.

sqlite_cache_size: int | None = None

As for Cache, per connection.

wal_size_limit: int | None = None

As for Cache, per shard (each shard has its own write-ahead log).

wal_checkpoint: Literal["manual", "auto"] = "manual"

As for Cache.

on_decode_error: Literal["raise", "miss"] | Callable[[str, Exception], object] | None = None

As for Cache.

durable: bool = False

As for Cache: single-key calls on a shard that fails give their miss values. One report covers every shard, named by the root directory.

raise_on_mismatch: bool = False

Raise LayoutMismatchError (a ValueError) when shards differs from the root’s recorded count, instead of using the recorded count with a warning (default False). It covers the count only: a root in another on-disk format still opens in its diskcache-oxide-format-N subdirectory.





Raises


 ValueError

A setting is out of range, or max_connections is below shards.

 LayoutMismatchError

shards differs from the root’s and raise_on_mismatch is True; or it differs, and a size_limit or max_connections that fits shards doesn’t split over the root’s count; or the directory belongs to a plain Cache (or a shard of it does). Also a ValueError, and a FormatMismatchError.

 TypeError

An argument has the wrong type, including a bool for timeout or shards.

 FormatMismatchError

Inside the versioned subdirectory, the manifest or a shard’s database is in a format this version can’t read (another format at the root itself opens the subdirectory instead).

 OSError

The filesystem doesn’t support hard links, which creating the manifest needs, or the process can’t open enough files for every shard (ulimit -n).

 Timeout

A shard stayed locked, or a fork stayed pending, for longer than timeout.





Examples
from diskcache_oxide import FanoutCache

cache = FanoutCache('/var/cache/my-app-counters', shards=8)   # shards is keyword-only
cache.incr('ip:203.0.113.7')          # as on Cache, on the key's shard
cache.shard_of('ip:203.0.113.7')      # 0 to 7, the same in every process and release
with cache.transact(key='totals') as tx:   # one shard's write lock, not all of them
    tx.set('totals', tx.get('totals', 0) + 1)

title: FanoutCache.memoize()
text:
Return a decorator that caches the function’s results in this cache, as diskcache’s memoize.


Usage
Source


FanoutCache.memoize(name=None, typed=False, expire=None, tag=None, ignore=())


A call’s key is (name,) + args + (None,) and then each keyword argument’s name and value, sorted by name, where name defaults to the function’s module and qualified name: the same tuple diskcache builds, which wrapper.__cache_key__(*args, **kwargs) returns. Arguments aren’t bound to the signature, so f(1, 2) and f(1, b=2) are two entries. A miss runs the function and stores its result (None included; an exception stores nothing); reads and writes pass retry=True. Call it: @cache.memoize(), not @cache.memoize.


Parameters


name: str | None = None

The key’s first element, in place of the function’s qualified name.

typed: bool = False

Also key on each argument’s type, as 'module.qualname' (D-045), so f(1) and f(1.0) are two entries.

expire: float | None = None

Seconds until a stored result expires; None never. Zero or negative never stores, as in diskcache.

tag: Key = None

The tag every stored result gets, for evict(tag): a key type, checked here.

ignore: Iterable[int | str] = ()

Positions and keyword names left out of the key.





Raises


 TypeError

name is callable (the decorator was used without parentheses), tag isn’t a key type, the function is async def, or, at a call, an argument isn’t a key type (D-048).

 ValueError

at a call, an argument is a NaN or a tuple nested too deep (D-048).





Examples
@cache.memoize(expire=300)
def episode(number: int) -> dict:
    return load_episode(number)

cache.delete(episode.__cache_key__(42))  # forget one call

title: FanoutCache.expire()
text:
Remove every expired entry from every shard, and its value file, as Cache.expire does.


Usage
Source


FanoutCache.expire(*, timeout=None, retry=False)


Parameters


timeout: float | None = None

Seconds the whole call may spend waiting for write locks (another thread’s or another process’s) or a pending fork, across every shard, for this call only (default: the cache’s timeout). It bounds waiting, not work: a chunk already running finishes, and once it’s spent, each remaining chunk still gets one try with no wait, so shards no one else is writing are all done even at a short timeout.

retry: bool = False

On a Timeout, try again until the call gets through, each round with the whole timeout, a durable=True handle included. Only Timeout is retried.





Returns


 int

How many entries were removed.





Raises


 Timeout

Some shard stayed locked past timeout; the others were still done. It carries removed and failed_shards (see the class docs), as any failure here does, under durable=True too.





Examples
try:
    cache.expire(timeout=5.0)
except Timeout as exc:
    exc.failed_shards, exc.removed   # which shards were skipped, and how many entries went anyway

text:
A registry of named caches under one base directory.


Usage
Source


Caches(
    base_dir,
    *,
    on_open_error=None,
    retry_open_after=10.0,
    _monotonic=time.monotonic,
    **defaults
)


Caches[Literal['general', 'show_pages']] makes a misspelled name a type error.


Parameters


base_dir: str | os.PathLike[str]

Where the caches live: each one in base_dir/<name> unless register says otherwise. Created when the first cache opens.

on_open_error: Callable[[str, Exception], object] | None = None

Called as on_open_error(name, exc) when a cache can’t open (default: log at ERROR on the diskcache_oxide logger, or at WARNING with no traceback for a Timeout). Whatever it raises is logged.

Seconds before a cache that failed to open is tried again (default 10). Lookups in between get a NullCache without trying. A Timeout means busy rather than broken, so that’s tried again after at most 1 s.

**defaults: Any

caches.register('rate_limits', shards=8)

caches.fanout('rate_limits').incr('ip:203.0.113.7')

title: Cache.stats()
text:
(hits, misses) of get and cache[key] in this process, as diskcache’s stats().


Usage
Source


Cache.stats(enable=True, reset=False)


Returns the counts as they were, then resets them if reset, then turns counting on or off with enable (off by default). Counted per process and in memory, never in the database, so a read never writes: other processes’ lookups aren’t included, the counts start from zero when the process (or a forked child) starts, and every handle on one directory in a process shares them. in, pop and iteration don’t count; a durable outage answered as a miss counts as nothing. A FanoutCache sums its shards.

title: Cache.set()
text:
Store value under key, replacing any existing value.


Usage
Source


Cache.set(key, value, expire=None, *, tag=None, retry=False)


Values of 64 KiB or more (after encoding) are stored in their own file.


Parameters


key: Key

The key.

value: Any

The value: str, bytes, numbers, Decimal, bool, None, and lists, tuples, dicts, sets, frozensets, datetimes and dates of those, or anything picklable with pickle=True.

expire: float | None = None

Seconds until the entry expires, or None for never.

tag: Key = None

A label for the entry, which evict(tag) removes by: any value a key can be, compared by exact type, so 1, 1.0 and True are three tags. None for none. An overwrite replaces the old tag, so an overwrite without one leaves the entry untagged.

retry: bool = False

On a Timeout, try again until the call gets through, each round with the whole timeout, a durable=True handle included. Only Timeout is retried.





Returns


 bool

True. With durable=True, False if the write failed and was dropped: whatever was
stored under key stays, and can be served stale.





Raises


 TypeError

The value can’t be stored exactly without pickle, expire is a bool, or tag isn’t a valid key type.

 Timeout

Another process held the write lock for longer than timeout.





Examples
cache.set('episodes:popular', episodes, expire=300)   # expires in 5 minutes
cache.set('user:42:profile', profile, tag='user:42')  # evict('user:42') removes it
cache.set('config', {'retries': 3})                   # never expires

title: Cache.remove_old_formats()
text:
Remove the caches an older diskcache-oxide format left in this cache’s directory: the


Usage
Source


Cache.remove_old_formats()


directory’s own cache, when it’s in an older format than this release’s, and any diskcache-oxide-format-M subdirectory holding one. Returns the database files, manifests and directories removed (value files inside a removed value folder aren’t listed one by one); [] when there’s nothing old.
Warning: it doesn’t check whether a process running an older diskcache-oxide still uses those files. Call it once every old worker has stopped, after draining any work queue they share. If an old worker is still running, on Linux and macOS its cache can be corrupted until it restarts (errors such as “database disk image is malformed”, or wrong results, not just misses), as with rm -rf under it, and everything it kept there is lost. On Windows, files an old worker has open are left, with a warning, for a later call.
Never removed: a cache in this release’s format or a newer one, anything diskcache-oxide didn’t write, anything behind a symbolic link, a database this process has open, a cache whose format can’t be read, and an empty database that may still be being created (one in a subdirectory or a shard, or at the root under 10 minutes old). What was removed is logged at INFO, and what was left, with why, at WARNING, on the diskcache_oxide logger.


Raises


 OSError

The directory can’t be listed.

title: Cache.push()
text:
Push value onto a queue and return its key, as diskcache’s push.


Usage
Source


Cache.push(
    value, prefix=None, side="back", expire=None, *, tag=None, retry=False
)


With prefix=None the queue’s keys are ints, numbered from 500,000,000,000,000; with a prefix, str keys '{prefix}-' and 15 digits. side='back' takes the next number up, 'front' the next down. Only keys of exactly that shape belong to the queue: a float, an ordinary key that shares the prefix, or a nested prefix’s items are ignored (D-054), so use a prefix no other key starts with. The number is found and the item stored in one write transaction, so concurrent pushes in any process never collide, and a push never overwrites a key.


Parameters


value: Any

The value, as for set().

prefix: None = None

The queue’s name, or None for the int queue.

side: bool = "back"

'back' (the default) or 'front'.

expire: float | None = None

Seconds until the item expires, or None for never.

tag: Key = None

The item’s tag, as for set().

retry: bool = False

As for set().





Returns


 int | None | str | None | int | str | None

The item’s key. With durable=True, None if the write failed (nothing was stored).





Raises


 OverflowError

The queue’s numbers are used up on that side (D-057).

 ValueError

side isn’t 'front' or 'back'.

 TypeError

prefix isn’t a str or None, or as for set().





Examples
jobs = Cache('/var/lib/my-app/state/jobs', timeout=3.0, eviction_policy='none')
jobs.push({'episode': 512}, prefix='transcode')   # 'transcode-500000000000000'

title: Cache.pop()
text:
Remove key and return its value, delivering it to exactly one caller.


Usage
Source


Cache.pop(key, default=None, *, expire_time=False, tag=False, retry=False)


Reads and decodes the value first, as get does, then deletes exactly that stored version, so a value it can’t read stays for whoever can. A pop that loses that delete to other writers 8 times falls back to removing the row first and decoding afterwards. Only then can a failed decode cost the value: one from a newer version, or any error from a pickle hook. timeout covers the whole call.


Parameters


key: Key

The key.

default: Any = None

Returned when the key is missing or expired, or its value file is missing.

expire_time: bool = False

Also return the entry’s expiry time.

tag: bool = False

Also return the entry’s tag.

retry: bool = False

On a Timeout, try again until the call gets through, each round with the whole timeout, a durable=True handle included. Only Timeout is retried.





Returns


 Any | tuple[Any, float | None] | tuple[Any, Key] | tuple[Any, float | None, Key]

The removed value, or default; with expire_time or tag, a tuple as get returns.
With durable=True, a pop whose delete fails returns
default, never the value, which could otherwise be delivered twice. The row stays.





Raises


 UnsafeValueError

The value was stored with pickle and this cache has pickle=False. The row stays.

 ForeignValueError

on_decode_error='raise', and another version or host might read the value. The row stays.

 CorruptValueError

on_decode_error='raise', and no build could read the value. The row is deleted first.

 Timeout

Another process held the write lock for longer than timeout, or timeout ran out after losing a race to another writer. This pop deletes nothing, and whatever the other writer left stays.





Examples
token = cache.pop('reset-token:abc')   # None if it was missing or already used

title: Cache.iterkeys()
text:
Iterate over keys in sorted order, optionally only those starting with prefix.


Usage
Source


Cache.iterkeys(*, prefix, reverse=False)


A prefix is an indexed range scan, so it costs time in proportion to the matches, not the size of the cache. Keys are fetched a page at a time with no lock held in between, so deleting keys while iterating is safe. Expired entries are skipped, whether or not their rows have been removed yet (D-060). Like a generator, an iterator serves one thread at a time: next() raises ValueError while another thread is inside it.


Parameters


prefix: str

Only yield keys that start with this string.

reverse: bool = False

Yield keys in descending order.





Returns


 Iterator[str] | Iterator[Key]

An iterator of keys.





Examples
for key in cache.iterkeys(prefix='user:42:'):   # an indexed range scan, sorted
    cache.delete(key)
newest_first = cache.iterkeys(reverse=True)

title: Cache.check()

Cache.check(fix=False, retry=False)


Reports, as a list of warnings.WarningMessage (nothing is issued through warnings): lines of SQLite’s integrity_check; a spilled entry whose value file is missing or the wrong size (file not found: ..., wrong file size: ...); a file in a value folder, or the cache directory, that no entry names and that is over an hour old (unknown file: ..., an UnknownFileWarning; a younger one may be a writer’s in flight); and stored totals that don’t match the rows. VACUUM writes the whole database through the write-ahead log and needs a temporary copy of it in SQLITE_TMPDIR, TMPDIR or /tmp; forks and writers wait for it.

Inside this thread’s own transact() block.

A step waited longer than timeout (and retry is False).

title: Sharing a cache across web workers
text: Deployment is where a cache meets the real world: several worker processes that don’t know each other’s names, a server that forks and recycles them while they’re busy, a cron job that opens the same directory on the side. diskcache-oxide is built for exactly this, so there isn’t much to it. This page gives one setup that works, then covers the few choices that matter. The example app runs this setup end to end.

title: Sharing a cache across web workers
text:

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI

from myapp.caching import close_everything


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    yield
    close_everything()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
In async code, reads can run on the event loop and writes go through asyncio.to_thread: see asyncio.

title: Sharing a cache across web workers
text:
Django
diskcache-oxide doesn’t ship a Django cache backend yet. One is next on the roadmap; until then, django.core.cache keeps whatever it has. Put the setup in a module of its own (myapp/caching.py), take ROOT from settings, and import it where it’s needed.
crumbs: Sharing a cache across web workers

title: Sharing a cache across web workers
text:
Celery and other background workers
Celery’s prefork pool, RQ and multiprocessing with the fork start method are pre-forking servers like gunicorn: import the setup at import time, and each child gets its own connections on first use. Register your types the same way the web workers do, or a worker that reads a web worker’s value gets ForeignValueError (or, on a durable cache, a miss and a logged warning, so every read of it goes to the source). Closing at shutdown is optional; Celery’s worker_process_shutdown signal is the place for it.
from celery.signals import worker_process_shutdown

from myapp.caching import close_everything


@worker_process_shutdown.connect
def close_caches(**kwargs) -> None:
    close_everything()
crumbs: Sharing a cache across web workers

title: Sharing a cache across web workers
text:
Pre-forking and spawning servers
With gunicorn (including --preload) or Celery’s prefork pool, it doesn’t matter whether you open the cache before or after the fork. diskcache-oxide’s fork barrier makes sure no worker starts life holding half a database transaction, and each child opens its own fresh connections on first use. See Concurrency and forks.
uvicorn --workers doesn’t fork: it starts each worker as a fresh process (the spawn start method, on every platform), so each worker imports your app and opens its caches itself. On Linux, multiprocessing defaults to the forkserver start method since Python 3.14, which behaves the same way. Either is fine; there’s nothing to configure.

title: Testing code that uses a cache
text:
Code that uses a cache has a talent for passing its tests for the wrong reason: the second assertion was green because the first one left the answer behind, and the test that “covers” expiry sleeps for two seconds and hopes. Such code needs tests of two kinds: tests where caching shouldn’t get in the way, and tests of the caching behavior itself (is the value cached, does it expire, is it invalidated). diskcache-oxide gives you a tool for each, and neither involves sleeping.

A real cache per test
A Cache in pytest’s tmp_path is fast and isolated: each test gets its own empty cache, and it’s thrown away afterwards.
import pytest

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

@pytest.fixture
def cache(tmp_path):
    with Cache(tmp_path / 'cache') as cache:
        yield cache


No caching at all: NullCache
For tests that exercise your app rather than its caching, a cached value from an earlier test can hide a bug. Swap in a NullCache: every read misses and every write succeeds, so every call goes to the real code path. It has the same methods and signatures as Cache, so nothing else changes.
from diskcache_oxide import NullCache

@pytest.fixture
def app_cache(monkeypatch):
    null = NullCache()
    monkeypatch.setattr('my_app.services.cache', null)
    return null
One thing a NullCache can’t catch: it never encodes values, so a set() of a value a real cache refuses (a dataclass you haven’t registered, an ORM row, a dict subclass) succeeds on a NullCache and raises TypeError in production. Keep at least one test per type you store that runs against a real Cache on tmp_path, using the cache fixture above. It’s also how you find out a type needs register_type.


Testing expiry without sleeping
diskcache-oxide reads the clock natively in Rust, so patching time.time doesn’t affect it on its own. Pass clock= instead. A small fake clock lets a test jump forward in time:

import tempfile

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

class FakeClock:
    def __init__(self, now: float = 1_000_000.0) -> None:
        self.now = now

    def __call__(self) -> float:
        return self.now

    def advance(self, seconds: float) -> None:
        self.now += seconds

clock = FakeClock()
cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=clock)

cache.set('session:abc', {'user': 42}, expire=30)
clock.advance(29)
print('after 29 s:', cache.get('session:abc'))
clock.advance(2)
print('after 31 s:', cache.get('session:abc'))

after 29 s: {'user': 42}
after 31 s: None


As a fixture:
@pytest.fixture
def clock():
    return FakeClock()

@pytest.fixture
def cache(tmp_path, clock):
    with Cache(tmp_path / 'cache', clock=clock) as cache:
        yield cache

def test_sessions_expire(cache, clock):
    cache.set('session:abc', {'user': 42}, expire=30)
    clock.advance(31)
    assert cache.get('session:abc') is None
If your tests already patch time.time (with unittest.mock, freezegun or time-machine) and you want the cache to follow along, pass clock=lambda: time.time(). The lambda looks up time.time on every call, so it sees the patched version.


Testing code that runs in several processes
Code that relies on the cache being shared, like a job claim or a rate limit, can be tested for real: start processes with multiprocessing and point them at the same tmp_path directory. diskcache-oxide is safe with every start method, including fork.
import multiprocessing

def claim(directory: str) -> bool:
    with Cache(directory) as cache:
        return cache.add('job:nightly', 'claimed', expire=60)

def test_only_one_worker_claims_the_job(tmp_path):
    with multiprocessing.Pool(8) as pool:
        results = pool.map(claim, [str(tmp_path)] * 8)
    assert results.count(True) == 1
A Cache also pickles: the copy a multiprocessing worker receives reopens the same directory with the same options, so you can pass the cache itself instead of its path.

title: Single-use keys
text: At 2 a.m. a tired user double-clicks a password reset link, and two requests arrive on two workers a few milliseconds apart. Both find the token. Both accept it. Some things must happen exactly once however many times they’re asked for: a reset link is good for one click, a verification code for one entry, a payment request for one charge even when the client retries. Two cache calls are atomic across every worker on the machine, pop() and add(), and between them they cover all of these.

title: Single-use keys
section: Short codes need an attempt limit
text:
Short codes need an attempt limit
A six-digit verification code is guessable, so pair it with a counter, created with an expiry the way the rate limiting recipe does, and burn the code after a few wrong guesses:
def check_code(user_id: int, entered: str) -> bool:
    attempts_key = f'verify-attempts:{user_id}'
    code_key = f'verify-code:{user_id}'
    tokens.add(attempts_key, 0, expire=10 * 60)
    if tokens.incr(attempts_key) > 5:
        tokens.delete(code_key)                   # too many tries: the code is dead
        return False
    if tokens.get(code_key) != entered:
        return False
    return tokens.pop(code_key) == entered        # right, and good for one entry only
The last line uses pop() so that two requests entering the right code at the same moment can’t both pass: only one of them gets the code back.

title: Running a job once across workers
text:
At the top of the hour, eight gunicorn workers wake up at the same instant with the same idea: time for the hourly cleanup. Each one has its own copy of the scheduler, none of them knows the others exist, and the only thing they share is a cache directory. You want the job to run once, and it turns out the directory is enough.
add() stores a value only if the key is missing or expired, and it’s atomic across every thread and process using the cache directory. When several callers race to add the same key, exactly one gets True. That makes the key a claim on the job.

Claim the run
import os

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')

def hourly_cleanup() -> None:
    if not cache.add('job:hourly-cleanup', os.getpid(), expire=55 * 60):
        return  # another worker has it this hour
    remove_stale_sessions()
The expire is the important part. It decides when the job can be claimed again, and it’s also what saves you if the worker that claimed the job crashes halfway through: the claim expires and the next run goes ahead. Set it a little shorter than the schedule’s interval, so the next run is never blocked by the previous claim.
Storing os.getpid() (or a hostname and pid) as the value costs nothing and makes it easy to see who claimed the job: cache.get('job:hourly-cleanup').


See it work
Here eight threads race for the same claim. Processes behave the same way.

import tempfile
import threading

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())
winners = []
start = threading.Barrier(8)

def worker(n: int) -> None:
    start.wait()
    if cache.add('job:hourly-cleanup', n, expire=3300):
        winners.append(n)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(n,)) for n in range(8)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(f'{len(winners)} winner: worker {winners[0]}')
print('claim holds:', cache.get('job:hourly-cleanup'))

1 winner: worker 7
claim holds: 7




Jobs that should run once, then again as soon as they’re done
For work that isn’t on a fixed schedule (process the queue, rebuild the search index), use expire as a lease: a time limit after which a crashed worker’s claim lapses. Delete the key when the work finishes, so the next request can claim it right away.
def rebuild_search_index() -> None:
    if not cache.add('job:search-index', os.getpid(), expire=10 * 60):
        return
    try:
        do_rebuild()
    finally:
        cache.delete('job:search-index')
Make the lease comfortably longer than the job ever takes. If the job outlives it, a second worker can start a second copy.


Give claims their own small cache
Two things can make a claim vanish early, and both argue for keeping claims out of your main cache:

Switching caching off. A NullCache follows the rule “every entry expires the instant it’s written”, so its add() always returns True. With caching off, every worker’s claim succeeds and the job runs once per worker. That’s harmless for idempotent jobs and wrong for jobs with side effects, like sending email.
Eviction. When a cache is over its size_limit, it evicts the least recently stored entries, and a claim is exactly the kind of small, rarely written entry that goes first. If it’s evicted before it expires, a second worker can claim the job.

A separate cache directory just for coordination, which is never swapped for a NullCache and never evicts (eviction_policy='none', so only expired claims go), avoids both:
coordination = Cache('/var/lib/my-app/state/coordination', timeout=3.0, eviction_policy='none')
A claim is the right tool when a worker that loses should skip the job. When it should wait its turn instead, use a Lock or a BoundedSemaphore from Coordination, on the same coordination cache.

title: Watching a cache in production
text:
A cache runs inside your workers for weeks without anyone looking at it, until a page gets slow or the disk fills up and someone asks whether the cache is working. Is it full? Is anything hitting it? Is the write-ahead log eating the disk? The numbers that answer those questions are cheap to read, so put them on a health endpoint or an admin page before you need them.

A health check
Everything here reads a few numbers and never waits on writers, so it’s fine to call on every health probe:

import os
import tempfile

from diskcache_oxide import Cache, CacheLike

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), size_limit=64 * 2**20)
cache.stats(enable=True)  # at startup, in every worker: counting is off until something turns it on

def wal_bytes(cache: CacheLike) -> int:
    if cache.directory is None:  # a NullCache
        return 0
    try:
        return os.path.getsize(os.path.join(cache.directory, 'diskcache-oxide.sqlite-wal'))
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return 0

def cache_health(cache: CacheLike) -> dict:
    hits, misses = cache.stats()
    lookups = hits + misses
    volume = cache.volume()
    return {
        'enabled': cache.enabled,
        'entries': len(cache),
        'volume_mib': round(volume / 2**20, 1),
        'percent_of_limit': round(100 * volume / cache.size_limit, 1),
        'eviction_policy': cache.eviction_policy,
        'hits': hits,
        'misses': misses,
        'hit_ratio': round(hits / lookups, 2) if lookups else None,
        'wal_mib': round(wal_bytes(cache) / 2**20, 1),
    }

for n in range(200):
    cache.set(f'page:{n}', 'x' * 20_000)
for n in range(300):
    cache.get(f'page:{n}')

print(cache_health(cache))

{'enabled': True, 'entries': 200, 'volume_mib': 3.9, 'percent_of_limit': 6.2, 'eviction_policy': 'least-recently-stored', 'hits': 200, 'misses': 100, 'hit_ratio': 0.67, 'wal_mib': 3.9}


Return it from an endpoint and you have something to graph or alert on. In Flask:
@app.get('/health/cache')
def health_cache() -> dict:
    return cache_health(cache)
In FastAPI the same function body works under @app.get('/health/cache'). Keep the endpoint behind your admin auth or on an internal port: the numbers aren’t secret, but there’s no reason to publish them.
In Kubernetes or behind a load balancer, use it as a readiness check, never a liveness check. A liveness failure restarts the process, and a cache outage is exactly what durable=True absorbs: restarting for it only adds a cold start.


What the numbers mean

enabled is False for a NullCache. If the cache comes from a Caches registry, that’s what a lookup hands out while the cache can’t open, so enabled: false on a cache you never switched off means something is wrong. The log says what.
len(cache) counts live entries: an entry stops counting the moment it expires, even before its row is removed. It’s a stored total less the expired rows still on disk, so it costs the same on a cache of ten entries or ten million, plus a little for each expired entry nothing has removed yet.
volume() is the cache’s size in bytes: the database pages in use plus the value files. It leaves out the write-ahead log and pages freed by deletes, which SQLite keeps in the file for reuse, so du on the directory can show more. check(fix=True) (below) gives the freed pages back.
size_limit and eviction_policy. Under the default 'least-recently-stored', a full cache sits close to its limit, and that’s normal: each set() that finds it over the limit evicts the oldest entries. Under 'none' nothing is evicted for size, so percent_of_limit can pass 100. On a sessions or work queue cache, that’s the number to alert on. Both attributes are the values this process last saw; cache.reset('size_limit') and cache.reset('eviction_policy') read what’s stored now, in case another process changed them.
Hits and misses count get and cache[key] in this process. An expired entry, and a value answered as a miss by on_decode_error, count as misses. in, pop and iteration don’t count, and a durable=True outage answered as a miss counts as nothing. A FanoutCache sums its shards, and a NullCache always reports (0, 0).

A low hit ratio on a full 'least-recently-stored' cache can mean size_limit is too small for what you’re caching: entries are evicted before anyone reads them twice. Raise it with cache.reset('size_limit', 2 * 2**30), which every process picks up at its next write, or in the constructor for the next deploy.


Hits and misses across workers
The counts live in each process’s memory and are never written to the database, so reading them costs nothing. That also means a health probe that lands on one gunicorn worker sees that worker’s counts only, since its last restart; a forked child starts from zero. Every handle on one directory in a process shares one set of counts, and they survive closing the last handle.
For a total across workers, have each worker add its counts to a shared counter now and then, from a timer or after every few hundred requests. Keep those counters in a small cache of their own, so reading the totals doesn’t count as lookups in the cache you’re measuring:

counters = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())

def publish_stats(cache: Cache, counters: Cache) -> None:
    hits, misses = cache.stats(reset=True)
    counters.incr('pages:hits', hits)
    counters.incr('pages:misses', misses)

publish_stats(cache, counters)
cache.get('page:1')
publish_stats(cache, counters)
print('every worker:', counters.get('pages:hits'), 'hits,', counters.get('pages:misses'), 'misses')
print('this worker since:', cache.stats())

every worker: 201 hits, 100 misses
this worker since: (0, 0)


stats(reset=True) returns the counts and zeroes them in one call, so a lookup between the read and the reset isn’t lost. This is the counters recipe applied to the cache itself.


An admin page for every cache
A Caches registry gives you one row per cache with stats(). It opens each registered cache, and never raises: a cache that can’t be opened gets its error set, with the exception’s type and message.

import dataclasses

from diskcache_oxide import Caches

caches = Caches(tempfile.mkdtemp(), timeout=1.0)
caches.register('general')
caches.register('pages', size_limit=256 * 2**20)
caches['general'].set('greeting', 'hello')

for name, stat in caches.stats().items():
    print(dataclasses.asdict(stat) | {'directory': '...'})

{'name': 'general', 'directory': '...', 'enabled': True, 'count': 1, 'volume': 40960, 'error': None}
{'name': 'pages', 'directory': '...', 'enabled': True, 'count': 0, 'volume': 40960, 'error': None}


A cache that can’t open shows up here with count and volume at 0 and the reason in error, for example LayoutMismatchError: ... for a directory that holds the other kind of cache. An upgrade that changed the on-disk format doesn’t: the cache opens in its versioned subdirectory. Watch for that with the warning instead. A diskcache_oxide record at WARNING saying a directory “holds a cache made by an older diskcache-oxide” (or “still holds”) means old files are waiting for remove_old_formats(), and “made by a newer diskcache-oxide” means a process is running an older release than the one that wrote the cache (see Upgrading across a format change).
As an endpoint, with each cache’s hit counts added. Every cache in this registry is a plain one; read a sharded one with caches.fanout(name) instead, since caches[name] raises TypeError for it:
@app.get('/admin/caches')
def admin_caches() -> dict:
    rows = {}
    for name, stat in caches.stats().items():
        hits, misses = caches[name].stats()
        rows[name] = dataclasses.asdict(stat) | {'hits': hits, 'misses': misses}
    return rows

@app.post('/admin/caches/<name>/clear')
def clear_cache(name: str) -> dict:
    return {'removed': caches.clear(name, timeout=10)}
caches.clear() raises if the cache can’t be opened, so the page never reports “0 removed” for a failure. It works on a disabled cache too. Give it a longer timeout= than the request path’s, since it holds the write lock once per chunk. For the rest of the registry’s admin calls, see Admin and shutdown.


Prometheus
A custom collector reads the registry at scrape time, so there’s nothing to update on each request. Entry counts and sizes come from the caches themselves, so every worker reports the same numbers and gunicorn’s Prometheus multiprocess mode isn’t needed for them:
from prometheus_client.core import REGISTRY, GaugeMetricFamily


class CacheCollector:
    def collect(self):
        entries = GaugeMetricFamily('app_cache_entries', 'Entries in each cache', labels=['cache'])
        size = GaugeMetricFamily('app_cache_bytes', 'Bytes on disk for each cache', labels=['cache'])
        up = GaugeMetricFamily('app_cache_up', '1 if the cache opened, 0 if not', labels=['cache'])
        for name, stat in caches.stats().items():
            entries.add_metric([name], stat.count)
            size.add_metric([name], stat.volume)
            up.add_metric([name], 0 if stat.error else 1)
        yield from (entries, size, up)


REGISTRY.register(CacheCollector())
Hit and miss counts are per process (stats() counts in memory), so under several workers a scrape sees only the worker that answered it. Count them in the cache itself if you need them across workers: Hits and misses across workers above shows how.


The write-ahead log
wal_mib in the health check is the size of diskcache-oxide.sqlite-wal beside the database. At normal load wal_size_limit keeps it at a few MiB. A burst of writes with readers in other processes can leave it much larger, and in the default wal_checkpoint='manual' mode it stays that size until something checkpoints it.
If it keeps growing, call checkpoint() from a maintenance job. It returns True when the log was copied into the database and truncated, and False, without raising, when other processes kept it busy; try again later. If that isn’t enough, open the cache with wal_checkpoint='auto'. Storage and WAL has the details. A FanoutCache has one log per shard, in the shard folders (000/, 001/, …), so add those up for the total.


Checking for damage
check() compares the database with the value files and returns what it found as a list of warnings.WarningMessage, without issuing any warnings. An empty list means nothing is wrong. Here a value file is deleted behind the cache’s back:

import glob

damaged = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())
damaged.set('report', b'x' * 100_000)   # 64 KiB or more: stored in a file of its own
damaged.set('summary', 'small')
[path] = glob.glob(os.path.join(damaged.directory, '*', '*.val'))
os.remove(path)                          # what a bad disk or a stray rm would do

for warning in damaged.check():
    print(warning.category.__name__, str(warning.message).replace(damaged.directory, '...'))
print('repaired:', len(damaged.check(fix=True)), '| after:', damaged.check(), '| entries:', len(damaged))

UserWarning file not found: .../7f/7f77e9498e4a6725cfe1eeaa0130bdf7.val
repaired: 1 | after: [] | entries: 1


It reports SQLite’s integrity_check lines, value files that are missing or the wrong size, files nobody owns that are over an hour old, and stored totals that don’t match the rows. check(fix=True) also repairs: it removes entries whose files are missing or cut short (they read as misses anyway), removes unowned files in the value folders, corrects the totals, then runs VACUUM, which shrinks the database file to what’s in use, and checkpoints.
Run it from a scheduled job one worker claims, never from a health probe. integrity_check reads the whole database and VACUUM rewrites it, and writers and forks wait for both. VACUUM also needs room for a temporary copy of the database in SQLITE_TMPDIR, TMPDIR or /tmp.
import logging

log = logging.getLogger('my_app')

def nightly_cache_check() -> None:
    problems = cache.check()
    for warning in problems:
        log.warning('cache check: %s', warning.message)
    if problems:
        cache.check(fix=True)


Log lines to alert on
Where diskcache-oxide has been told not to raise, it logs on the diskcache_oxide logger instead, and that line is then the only sign anything happened. Make sure the logger reaches your log aggregator or Sentry:

A Caches cache that can’t open logs at ERROR with the traceback, once per retry, and hands out a NullCache meanwhile. An open that only timed out logs at WARNING.
durable=True logs swallowed failures at most once a minute per cache handle, with counts by operation: WARNING for a busy lock, ERROR for a full disk, an I/O error or a failed delete.
on_decode_error='miss' logs a warning for a stored value it couldn’t read.
A cache whose directory holds another on-disk format logs a WARNING once per process: “holds a cache made by an older diskcache-oxide” (or “still holds”, while the old files remain), or “made by a newer diskcache-oxide” when a process runs an older release than the one that wrote it. The record carries directory, using, found and found_in. See Upgrading across a format change.
A FanoutCache whose folder has another shard count than shards= logs a WARNING once per process (the record carries directory, stored_shards and requested_shards), and a Caches registry logs its own WARNING and one ERROR per process.

The exact messages, and what to do about each, are in Errors and what to do about them.


Things to know

stats() turns counting on. Its enable argument defaults to True, so a health check that reads the counts also starts them. stats(enable=False) turns counting off and stops the counts where they are.
Counts reset on restart. Graph the hit ratio, not the raw counts, or publish the counts as above.
volume() includes expired entries until expire(), or the cleanup a set() does, removes them, though len() already leaves them out. A scheduled expire() frees their space; caches.expire_all() does every registered cache.
Health checks shouldn’t write. Everything in cache_health is a read. check() and checkpoint() belong in a maintenance job.

title: Recipes
text:
A shared cache does more jobs in a real app than caching. It elects a worker, counts requests, holds sessions and one-time tokens, remembers what was invalidated, and stands in for Redis wherever Redis was only ever there to hold a counter. Each recipe below starts with the moment you’d reach for one, then shows the pattern, then says where it stops working. The examples with output under them run against diskcache-oxide every time these docs are built, and the example app puts most of these recipes together in one FastAPI app, tested.

Caching
Caching expensive calls. The cache-aside pattern, and memoize, which turns a function into a cached one keyed on its arguments.
Serving stale values while refreshing. Keep a slow page or report available while one worker rebuilds it in the background, or refresh the hot keys ahead of time from a job, so readers never wait and the thundering herd is one worker.
Caching responses from other services. Cache an upstream API’s answers, honor its max-age, revalidate with ETags, and keep serving the last good answer when it’s down.
Invalidating groups of keys. Clear everything cached for one user, one product or one page at once: delete by key prefix, drop every entry with a tag using evict(tag), or bump a generation number so stale entries are never read again.
Storing your own types. UUIDs, enums, timedeltas, Paths, dataclasses and Pydantic models in the cache with one registration each, and no pickle.


Coordinating workers
For locks, semaphores and a throttle that hold across every process, see the Coordination guide page. The recipes here build on the same atomic calls.
Running a job once across workers. Eight gunicorn workers each schedule the same hourly job, and you want it to run once. add() is atomic across processes, so exactly one of them claims it.
Rate limiting. Count requests per client in fixed time windows with add() and incr(), shared by every worker on the machine, with no Redis.
Counting things. View counts, download totals and usage quotas with incr() and decr(), flushed to the database with pop() so no count is lost or doubled.
Work queues. A queue every worker on the machine shares: push() at one end, pull() from the other, each item delivered to exactly one worker.
Single-use keys. Reset links, verification codes and idempotency keys: pop() hands a value to exactly one caller, and add() accepts a key exactly once.


State
Server-side sessions. Sessions every worker can read, with a sliding idle timeout from touch(), an absolute lifetime, and log-out-everywhere by key prefix.


Deployment and testing
Sharing a cache across web workers. Where to put the cache directory, when to open it with gunicorn, uvicorn, FastAPI, Flask, Django and Celery, how to keep a busy cache from slowing requests, and what to do at shutdown.
Docker and Compose. One named volume for the caches and state, a fixed non-root user, the ownership rules that otherwise end in PermissionError, Kubernetes volumes, disk sizing, and the cleanup step after a format change.
Using the cache from asyncio. Read inline, write off the loop, and keep transactions on one thread, in FastAPI, Starlette or aiohttp.
Watching a cache in production. A health check and an admin endpoint: entries, bytes on disk, hit ratio across workers, the size limit, the write-ahead log, check() for damage, and the log lines worth alerting on.
Upgrading across a format change. When a release changes the on-disk format: the new release opens its own cache in a versioned subdirectory, old and new workers run side by side, remove_old_formats() cleans up afterwards, and what to do first about queues, counters and sessions.
Testing code that uses a cache. pytest fixtures for a real cache in a temporary directory, a NullCache for tests that shouldn’t cache at all, and a fake clock for testing expiry without sleeping.


In the user guide
Some features have more to them than a recipe can hold, so they have guide pages of their own: Coordination (locks, semaphores, throttle, barrier, Averager and memoize_stampede, which refreshes a hot value before it expires), FanoutCache for many writing processes, and Transactions. What’s coming next is on the roadmap.

title: Storing your own types
text:
The first TypeError from set() is a small shock. You’ve been storing dicts for weeks, and today one of them has a UUID in it and the cache says no. That refusal is the design: the cache stores the built-in types exactly (Serialization has the table: str, numbers, bytes, bool, None, lists, tuples, sets, dicts, datetime, date, Decimal) and refuses anything else rather than pickling it behind your back. For everything else, you tell the codec once how to store the type, and the shock never comes back. This recipe collects the registrations a typical web app needs.

The standard library’s types
uuid.UUID, datetime.timedelta and pathlib.Path aren’t built-in types to the codec. Each needs an encode that turns an instance into something storable and a decode that turns it back:

import datetime
import pathlib
import tempfile
import uuid

import diskcache_oxide
from diskcache_oxide import Cache

diskcache_oxide.register_type(uuid.UUID, name='std.uuid', encode=lambda u: u.bytes, decode=lambda b: uuid.UUID(bytes=b))
diskcache_oxide.register_type(datetime.timedelta, name='std.timedelta', encode=datetime.timedelta.total_seconds, decode=lambda s: datetime.timedelta(seconds=s))
diskcache_oxide.register_type(type(pathlib.Path()), name='std.path', encode=str, decode=pathlib.Path)

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())
cache.set('upload', {'id': uuid.uuid4(), 'ttl': datetime.timedelta(hours=2), 'file': pathlib.Path('/srv/uploads/a.png')})
print({k: type(v).__name__ for k, v in cache.get('upload').items()})

{'id': 'UUID', 'ttl': 'timedelta', 'file': 'PosixPath'}


The Path registration says type(pathlib.Path()), not pathlib.Path, for a reason: lookup is by exact type, and pathlib.Path() builds a PosixPath or a WindowsPath. Registering the base class would match nothing. The same applies to any factory that returns a subclass.


Enums
Store the value, and let the enum class turn it back into a member. A StrEnum or IntEnum is a subclass of str or int, and a subclass is never stored as its base, so it needs this too:

import enum

class Plan(enum.StrEnum):
    FREE = 'free'
    PRO = 'pro'

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Plan, name='app.Plan', encode=lambda p: p.value, decode=Plan)

cache.set('account:42:plan', Plan.PRO)
print(repr(cache.get('account:42:plan')))

<Plan.PRO: 'pro'>




Dataclasses
A dataclass needs only a name. Its fields are stored and it’s rebuilt with cls(**fields), so defaults and __post_init__ run. Fields can hold other registered types, nested as deep as you like:

import dataclasses

@dataclasses.dataclass
class Invoice:
    id: uuid.UUID
    plan: Plan
    issued: datetime.date
    paid_within: datetime.timedelta | None = None

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Invoice, name='app.Invoice')

cache.set('invoice:latest', Invoice(uuid.UUID('2b7e1c4a-5d3f-4e8b-9a6c-0f1d2e3a4b5c'), Plan.PRO, datetime.date(2026, 11, 8)))
print(cache.get('invoice:latest'))

Invoice(id=UUID('2b7e1c4a-5d3f-4e8b-9a6c-0f1d2e3a4b5c'), plan=<Plan.PRO: 'pro'>, issued=datetime.date(2026, 11, 8), paid_within=None)




Pydantic models
Pydantic can produce and consume a plain dict, so a model registers with its own two methods. mode='json' makes model_dump() emit only JSON-compatible values (UUIDs and dates as strings), which model_validate() parses back, so the model’s field types need no registrations of their own:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class User(BaseModel):
    id: uuid.UUID
    name: str
    plan: Plan

diskcache_oxide.register_type(User, name='app.User', encode=lambda u: u.model_dump(mode='json'), decode=User.model_validate)
attrs classes and msgspec structs follow the same pattern with attrs.asdict() and msgspec.to_builtins(), and the class as the decoder.


Values only, never keys
A registration teaches the codec to store a type as a value. Keys, tags and the arguments of a memoized function are a separate, fixed set of types (str, bytes, int, float, bool, None and tuples of those), compared by exact type, and registering a class doesn’t add it to that set. A UUID, a Plan member (even though it’s a StrEnum) or an Invoice as a key raises TypeError. Convert at the edge, to the identifier the key needs:

invoice = cache.get('invoice:latest')

try:
    cache.set(invoice.id, invoice)
except TypeError as error:
    print(error)

cache.set(('invoice', str(invoice.id)), invoice)             # a UUID key, as a str
cache.set(('plan-limits', Plan.PRO.value), {'seats': 25})    # an enum key, by its value
print(cache.get(('invoice', str(invoice.id))).plan)

cache keys must be str, bytes, int, float, bool, None, or a tuple of those, not UUID
pro


A memoized function can return a registered type, so @cache.memoize() on a loader that returns an Invoice works once Invoice is registered. Its arguments still have to be key types, so take invoice_id: str rather than a UUID.


Where the registrations live
Registrations are process-wide and must exist in every process that opens the directory: the web workers, the Celery workers, the management command that warms the cache. A row written with a tag the reading process doesn’t know is a ForeignValueError, and the row is left for a process that does. Put them in one module and import it early:
# myapp/cache_types.py: imported from myapp/__init__.py, so every entry point gets it
import diskcache_oxide

from myapp.models import Invoice, Plan, User

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Plan, name='app.Plan', encode=lambda p: p.value, decode=Plan)
diskcache_oxide.register_type(Invoice, name='app.Invoice')
diskcache_oxide.register_type(User, name='app.User', encode=lambda u: u.model_dump(mode='json'), decode=User.model_validate)
A cache that needs its own encoding of a type can take a diskcache_oxide.TypeRegistry as types=, which it consults before the process-wide registry. The same rule applies: every process that opens that directory needs the same registrations.


When the shape changes
The name is the contract. Renaming or moving the class changes nothing, because rows carry the name you chose. Changing the fields does: a dataclass row written before a required field was added raises CorruptValueError when it’s read, and on_decode_error='miss' turns that into a miss and deletes the row, so the next writer replaces it. For a change the old rows can’t survive, give the type a new name (app.Invoice.v2). The old rows become ForeignValueError, treated as misses under the same policy, and expire on their own. See Errors.

title: Caching responses from other services
text:
Your dashboard endpoint takes 1.2 seconds, and 1.1 of them are spent waiting for a partner API to return the same JSON it returned to the previous request. An app that calls other services (a payments API, a headless CMS, your own microservices) spends most of its latency waiting on them, and most of those answers don’t change between calls. Caching them in a directory every worker shares means one request to the upstream per machine instead of one per worker, and a last known good answer to serve when the upstream is slow, or down, or has started returning the wrong thing with a 500.

A cached fetch
The entry holds the response body, its ETag and a freshness deadline taken from the upstream’s Cache-Control: max-age, with a default when there isn’t one. A fresh entry is returned without a request. A stale one is revalidated with If-None-Match, so an unchanged resource costs a 304 with no body. And if the request fails while there’s a stale entry, the stale entry is the answer.

import json
import re
import tempfile
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

import httpx

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

now = [1_000_000.0]                                   # a fake clock; in a real app use time.time()
cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=lambda: now[0])

def max_age(response: httpx.Response) -> float | None:
    m = re.search(r'max-age=(\d+)', response.headers.get('cache-control', ''))
    return float(m.group(1)) if m else None

def fetch_json(client: httpx.Client, url: str, *, default_ttl: float = 300, keep: float = 24 * 3600) -> object:
    key = ('http', 'GET', url)
    host = urlsplit(url).netloc                       # the tag, to drop one service's responses at once
    entry = cache.get(key)
    if entry is not None and now[0] < entry['fresh_until']:
        return json.loads(entry['body'])              # fresh: no request at all

    headers = {'If-None-Match': entry['etag']} if entry and entry['etag'] else {}
    try:
        response = client.get(url, headers=headers)
        if response.status_code != 304:
            response.raise_for_status()
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        if entry is not None:
            return json.loads(entry['body'])          # upstream trouble: the last good answer
        raise

    if response.status_code == 304:                   # unchanged: keep the body, extend its freshness
        entry['fresh_until'] = now[0] + (max_age(response) or default_ttl)
    else:
        entry = {
            'body': response.content,
            'etag': response.headers.get('etag'),
            'fresh_until': now[0] + (max_age(response) or default_ttl),
        }
    cache.set(key, entry, expire=keep, tag=host)
    return json.loads(entry['body'])

Here it runs against a mock upstream that counts its requests:

seen: list[str | None] = []

def upstream(request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
    seen.append(request.headers.get('If-None-Match'))
    headers = {'ETag': '"v1"', 'Cache-Control': 'max-age=60'}
    if request.headers.get('If-None-Match') == '"v1"':
        return httpx.Response(304, headers=headers)
    return httpx.Response(200, json={'episodes': [512, 513]}, headers=headers)

client = httpx.Client(transport=httpx.MockTransport(upstream))
url = 'https://api.example.com/episodes'

fetch_json(client, url)
fetch_json(client, url)                               # fresh: served from the cache
now[0] += 61
fetch_json(client, url)                               # stale: one conditional request, answered 304
print(f'{len(seen)} upstream requests; If-None-Match headers sent: {seen}')

2 upstream requests; If-None-Match headers sent: [None, '"v1"']


Why it’s shaped this way:

Freshness lives in the value, not in expire. The entry’s expire (keep) is how long a stale copy is worth holding on to for revalidation and outages. If freshness were the expiry, a stale entry would vanish just when it’s useful.
304 costs one small write. The body is kept and only fresh_until changes. A set() is needed because the deadline is inside the value; touch() only moves the entry’s expiry.
The key names the request. It’s a tuple of method and URL, so no string formatting is needed and a URL can’t run into the next field. If the response depends on who’s asking (an Authorization header, a tenant), add that identity to the tuple, ('http', 'GET', url, tenant_id), or one user’s data will be served to another.
Every set passes the tag. An overwrite without tag= leaves the entry untagged, so the 304 path tags its write too.



Dropping one service’s responses
Each entry is tagged with its upstream’s host, so when a service tells you its data changed (a CMS publish webhook, a deploy of your own microservice), evict drops everything cached from it in one call, whatever the URLs were:

fetch_json(client, 'https://api.example.com/episodes/512')
print(cache.evict('api.example.com'), 'responses removed')

2 responses removed


A tuple key has no string prefix, so iterkeys(prefix=...) can’t find these entries; the tag is how you reach them as a group. See Invalidating groups of keys.


Variations

Serving the bytes straight through. When your endpoint relays the upstream’s body, store response.content and the content-type, and return them as they are, without parsing. Bodies of 64 KiB or more are stored in their own file, so a large payload costs no more than a small one.
Negative caching. A 404 that costs a round trip every time is worth caching for a short while: store {'status': 404, 'fresh_until': ...} and return your own not-found from it. Don’t cache 5xx as answers; the stale-on-error path above already covers an upstream outage.
Headers not to keep. Drop Set-Cookie and anything else tied to the one connection before storing a response’s headers.
Only one worker should refetch. When many requests find the same stale entry at once, they all revalidate. 304s are cheap, so that’s usually fine. If the upstream charges per call, wrap the refetch in a claim as the stale-while-revalidate recipe does.

title: Using the cache from asyncio
text: An async framework makes one promise to every request it’s serving: nothing blocks the loop. A synchronous cache call looks like a small risk to that promise, and whether it is depends entirely on which call. diskcache-oxide’s API is synchronous. An AsyncCache is planned as an experiment, to ship only if it earns its place (see the roadmap), but the sync cache already works well in an asyncio app, provided you know which calls can block the event loop and for how long. Here are the three rules.

title: Using the cache from asyncio
text:
Fire and forget
When the response shouldn’t wait for the write at all, schedule it as a task. Keep a reference to the task until it finishes, or the loop may drop it half done:
background: set[asyncio.Task] = set()

def cache_later(key: str, value: object, expire: float) -> None:
    task = asyncio.create_task(asyncio.to_thread(cache.set, key, value, expire=expire))
    background.add(task)
    task.add_done_callback(background.discard)
