title: Changelog
text:
This changelog is generated automatically from GitHub Releases.

v0.3.5 (unreleased)
GitHub
Upgrades across a format change no longer fail. A cache directory that holds a cache in another on-disk format (made by an older release, or by a newer one before a rollback) now opens a new, empty cache in its subdirectory diskcache-oxide-format-N, N being this release’s format (3), instead of raising FormatMismatchError, and logs a warning on the diskcache_oxide logger once per process. Of the other format’s cache, only its format is read, and its contents are never changed (if that read is the last connection to close on it, SQLite may checkpoint its write-ahead log into the database file, which changes no data). Once the subdirectory exists, every later open uses it. A FanoutCache moves as a whole. This release keeps format 3, so caches made by 0.2.3 open where they are, warm; a cache still at format 2 (0.1.2) opens diskcache-oxide-format-3 beside it. See “Upgrading across a format change” in the recipes.

Added

remove_old_formats() on Cache, FanoutCache and NullCache (where it returns []), and on Caches for every registered cache: removes caches in an older format from the cache’s directory, only files diskcache-oxide wrote, never following links, never a newer or the current format, and returns what it removed. It doesn’t check whether an older worker still uses those files: call it once they’ve all stopped.
Windows on x86_64, with wheels for CPython 3.14, 3.14t, 3.15 and 3.15t. The API and the on-disk format are the same; caches made on macOS or Linux aren’t affected. Windows has no fork(), so the fork guarantees are Unix-only. Getting started has a new Windows section: an open cache’s directory can’t be deleted, new directories inherit their parent’s permissions, and a value file another program holds past about 50 ms of retries is left until check(fix=True) removes it, an hour after it was written. SQLite uses its own Win32 mutexes there (_sqlite_mutex_status() reports 'native').



Changed

A cache directory holding another on-disk format opens the diskcache-oxide-format-N subdirectory with a warning instead of raising FormatMismatchError (D-059). FormatMismatchError is now raised only for another format inside that subdirectory. directory on Cache and FanoutCache reports where the cache really is, the subdirectory after such a move; a pickled handle keeps the directory as passed and resolves it again. A Caches registry no longer hands out a NullCache for a format change.
A plain Cache opened on a FanoutCache shard directory in an older format raises LayoutMismatchError, as it always did for a current one, rather than FormatMismatchError.
FanoutCache(directory, shards=n) on a root that records another count no longer raises: it opens with the stored count and logs a WARNING once per process. The new keyword raise_on_mismatch=True restores the LayoutMismatchError, and Caches.register(..., raise_on_mismatch=True) turns it into an open failure (a reported NullCache). A root in another on-disk format redirects to its versioned subdirectory either way. The LayoutMismatchError for settings that don’t fit the stored count now says shards=n was asked for rather than is registered with, since a plain FanoutCache raises it too.
len(), iterkeys(), iter() and reversed() leave out an entry the moment it expires, as get and in already did, on Cache and FanoutCache (D-060). Before, an expired entry was counted and listed until a set(), expire() or cull() removed its row, so a cache that’s mostly read could report entries nobody could read. Nothing is written by the check; the rows and their space, in volume(), still go only when something removes them, so a scheduled expire() is still how a mostly-read cache frees space. len() now also counts the expired rows not yet removed, through the expiry index, so it costs a little more while such rows are waiting.



Fixed

import diskcache_oxide no longer calls os.register_at_fork where it doesn’t exist.
A value file that hits a full quota (EDQUOT) now raises OSError with errno.ENOSPC, as a full disk does, since a full disk is recognized by the error’s kind rather than one Unix error number.
iter(cache) and reversed(cache) no longer sort the whole table for every page of keys. Without SQLite statistics, the planner read insertion order through the key index and sorted it, so walking a large cache took time in proportion to its size for every 512 keys (about 2 s for 200,000 entries on an M5 Max, now 22 ms); each page now seeks on the row id.



Documentation

An example app in examples/webapp: a FastAPI app with gunicorn, a background worker and Docker Compose, built the way the docs recommend, with tests that run it as real processes. Every page shows which cache reads served it.
One recommended production setup throughout the docs: a durable Caches registry with timeout=1.0 for data that can be rebuilt, and state (sessions, job claims, locks, queues) in plain caches opened directly, with eviction off, under one /var/lib/my-app directory. The Caches guide explains why state never goes through the registry.
New pages: Docker and Compose (volumes, a fixed UID, ownership, Kubernetes, disk sizing, backups, cleanup after a format change) and Troubleshooting (start from the symptom).
Corrected: the docs no longer claim network filesystems are detected at open. SQLite can’t tell, so keep caches on a local disk.
Also new: a keyword table and the state-copying loop in Switching from diskcache, Windows notes in Getting started, a Prometheus collector in Monitoring, a dictConfig that keeps the diskcache_oxide logger, and API reference sections for types, memoize, coordination and every error.




v0.2.3
2026-11-12 · GitHub
Delete your caches when you upgrade. This release changes the on-disk format (format 3, for tags and the eviction policy). Opening a cache made by 0.1.2 raises FormatMismatchError, naming the database: stop every process using the cache, delete its directory (a FanoutCache’s whole root, never one shard), and it’s recreated empty on the next open. 0.1.2 refuses a format-3 cache the same way, and neither version writes anything into the other’s. A 0.1.2 worker still running when its cache is deleted and recreated can’t change the new one either: once it opens the new file, its writes, deletes and maintenance calls fail with “no such table” (only a touch gets through), because format 3 renames the table they all use.

Added

Keys of every native type: bytes, int (64-bit), float, bool, None, and tuples of those, nested up to 32 deep, beside str. They’re never pickled and compare by exact type, so 1, 1.0 and True are three keys. iterkeys() lists str keys first, then the other types in a fixed order; iterkeys(prefix=...) lists str keys only. A FanoutCache routes every key type. Type checkers see diskcache_oxide.Key.
memoize(name=None, typed=False, expire=None, tag=None, ignore=()) on Cache, FanoutCache and NullCache, as diskcache’s, with the same keys, so f.__cache_key__(...) returns the tuple diskcache would. Every argument must be a key type, checked before the function runs; typed=True stores type names. Memoized and Memoizer type the wrapper.
CorruptKeyError, a CorruptValueError, raised by iteration that meets a stored key it can’t read (a damaged page or file); it never skips one.
reversed(cache), pop(key, expire_time=True), a read-only durable attribute, and reset(key, value) to read or persist size_limit, cull_limit and eviction_policy (a FanoutCache splits a size_limit total across its shards), on Cache, FanoutCache and NullCache.
Pickling a Cache or FanoutCache: it reopens the directory with the options the handle was opened with, in another process too. A TypeRegistry pickles (the global one by reference).
stats(enable=True, reset=False): hit and miss counts of get, per process and in memory, so a get never writes.
check(fix=False, retry=False): the database and value files against each other, as diskcache’s, in short steps; fix=True removes entries whose files are missing or cut short and old orphan files, sweeps empty folders, corrects the totals and VACUUMs. UnknownFileWarning and EmptyDirWarning.
The coordination recipes Lock, RLock, BoundedSemaphore, Averager, throttle, barrier and memoize_stampede, as diskcache’s, refusing a NullCache or durable=True cache, with throttle’s two diskcache bugs fixed. See the new Coordination guide page.
Tags: tag= (keyword-only) on set and add, any key type, compared by exact type, and tag=True on get and pop, returning diskcache’s (value, tag) and (value, expire_time, tag) tuples. evict(tag, *, timeout=None, retry=False) on Cache, FanoutCache and NullCache removes every entry with that tag stored before the call, in chunks like clear(). memoize(tag=...) and the recipes’ tag= tag what they store. An overwrite without tag= leaves the entry untagged; add on a live key, touch and incr keep its tag.
eviction_policy='least-recently-stored' (the default) or 'none' on Cache and FanoutCache, stored in the cache and read inside every write, so a change from one process applies to all at their next write. Under 'none' nothing is evicted for size, expired entries are still removed, and cull() returns how many it removed. 'least-recently-used' and 'least-frequently-used' raise ValueError. A read-only eviction_policy attribute.
The queue calls push, pull, peek and peekitem on Cache and NullCache, with diskcache’s signatures and return shapes (expire_time=, tag=, retry= keyword-only). Each item goes to exactly one puller across every process; pull decodes before it deletes, so an item this process can’t read stays queued; peek and peekitem never write. A queue’s items are only keys of its exact shape, and push raises OverflowError rather than overwrite a key. See the new Work queues recipe.
ENOVAL and UNKNOWN, diskcache’s sentinels.
retry=True (keyword-only) on get, set, add, delete, pop, touch, incr, decr, expire, cull, clear and evict: this cache’s own Timeout is retried until the call gets through, even on a durable=True handle; one raised by your code (a hook, a clock) is not. A retried expire, cull, clear or evict returns everything it removed.



Changed

Iterating a cache is typed Iterator[Key] rather than Iterator[str], since keys can now be other types; iterkeys(prefix=...) is still Iterator[str]. Type-checked code that treats every iterated key as a str needs a narrowing (isinstance(key, str)).
The TypeError for a key of the wrong type now names the types that are accepted.
TransactionalCacheLike gained push, pull, peek and peekitem (not CacheLike: FanoutCache has no queue calls).
CacheLike gained memoize, stats, check, reset, evict, durable, eviction_policy and __reversed__, get and pop their tag= (and pop its expire_time=), and set and add theirs; a fake typed against it needs them too.
transact(retry=True) sleeps between attempts instead of retrying at once, so a timeout=0 cache doesn’t spin.




v0.1.2
2026-11-09 · GitHub
The first release: diskcache’s Cache API on a Rust engine and SQLite storage, shared safely by threads, processes and fork(), on CPython 3.14 and 3.15 including the free-threaded builds. Wheels for macOS on Apple Silicon and Linux (glibc) on x86_64 and aarch64.

Added

Cache, API compatible with diskcache 5.6.3’s Cache: get, set, add, incr/decr, pop, delete, touch, expire, cull, clear, iterkeys, len, volume, size limits with least-recently-stored eviction, and the mapping methods. It passes a conformance suite run against diskcache itself, apart from the documented divergences.
FanoutCache, which shards keys over several databases so many writing processes don’t queue on one write lock.
transact() on both, which lands several writes together or none of them, with TransactionBusy and TransactionAborted.
Values stored as msgpack (the default) or JSON, with exact type tags for tuples, sets, datetimes, big ints and NaN. A value that can’t round-trip exactly raises TypeError at set(). register_type() stores your own types and a library’s without pickle, a dataclass with only a name; pickle=True is opt-in per cache, and a cache without it never unpickles.
durable=True, which answers an outage (a busy lock, a full disk) as a miss and logs it at most once a minute, and on_decode_error= for values that can’t be read.
NullCache, which turns caching off without changing call sites, and Caches, a registry that names an app’s caches, opens each on first use and hands out a NullCache while one can’t open.
Fork safety: a process-wide fork barrier so no child is born holding half a transaction, and caches that keep working in the child.
Bounded resources: at most max_connections SQLite connections per cache directory, a page cache per connection, a write-ahead log that trims itself back to half of wal_size_limit, and checkpoint().
CacheLike, TransactionalCacheLike and ShardedCacheLike protocols, py.typed, and full docstrings in the stubs.
A bundled SQLite (sqlite_version(), sqlite_compile_options()), so the system’s version doesn’t matter.
Documentation: a user guide, recipes, an errors page, an API reference, an agent skill and llms.txt, at https://mkennedy.codes/docs/diskcache-oxide/.



Differences from diskcache

Not data compatible: data lives in diskcache-oxide.sqlite, and diskcache’s cache.db is never opened or converted, so a switched app starts cold.
Keys are str only, directory is required, size_limit must be at least 1 MiB, new cache directories are owner-only (0700), Timeout is a TimeoutError, and bool(cache) is always True.
clear() keeps writes that land while it runs, expire() removes every expired entry, and a read during an overwrite never misses. Each is a diskcache bug, with a standalone repro in the repository’s upstream/ folder.



Not yet
memoize, tags, AsyncCache, Deque and Index, keys other than str, disk=, other eviction policies, the coordination recipes (locks, semaphores, throttles), and Windows. See the roadmap.
Development before this release, including the 0.1.0.dev builds (0.1.0.dev1 was yanked from PyPI), is in the git history. A 0.1.0 and a 0.1.1 were built and verified but never published: new tests found two bugs just before the first upload and a third (a size-limited cache evicting entries it had room for) just before the second, each fixed first, so 0.1.2 is the first release on PyPI. 0.1.1 ran in production at Talk Python in the meantime. The 0.0.1 on PyPI is a name placeholder with no code.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
diskcache-oxide
A shared, durable disk cache for Python, with a Rust engine, SQLite storage, and a diskcache-compatible API.
Python cache. Rust engine. SQLite storage.
Every Python web app arrives at the same crossroads. A query that was fine at launch is now the slowest thing on the page, so you cache its result in a dict, and for one afternoon you’re a hero. Then the app goes under gunicorn with four workers, and there are four dicts, each warming up alone and each forgetting everything the moment its worker is recycled. So you reach for Redis, and now there’s a server to deploy, secure, monitor and pay for, whose entire job is to remember the answer to one query.
python-diskcache showed there was a third road: a cache that is just a directory. Every thread and every process on the machine opens the same path and sees the same entries, and the entries are still there tomorrow, because a directory doesn’t restart. No daemon, no network hop, no second system to keep alive. It’s the kind of idea that sounds too simple to be fast, and for years that was the catch. diskcache itself has had no commits since 2023, and its issues and pull requests go unanswered.
diskcache-oxide removes the catch. It keeps the diskcache API you already know and rebuilds everything beneath it for where Python is going: many cores, many worker processes, free-threaded CPython, and async frameworks that can’t afford a slow call on the event loop. The engine is Rust. The storage is SQLite. The Python layer is as thin as it can be. One thread gets nearly 700,000 cache operations a second out of a Cache, and eight threads sharing it still get that rate while python-diskcache’s falls below 20,000. Nothing on your disk is a pickle unless you asked for one (increasing compatibility and security), and memory and disk use stay where you set them.
Source on GitHub: https://github.com/mikeckennedy/diskcache-oxide · Issues
Here is the whole idea on one screen. Four workers, one directory. The cache makes the slow query cheap, and add() elects exactly one worker to run the hourly job, because a write that’s atomic across processes is a lock if you squint:
And here is what it does under load. Every thread shares one cache, the x axis adds threads, and the two libraries go in opposite directions:

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
An app with several caches
Most apps end up with more than one cache: rendered pages, API responses, sessions, rate limits, each with its own size and settings. Caches is the registry for them. You register each cache once at startup, and a lookup by name opens it on first use and returns the same object every time after that. If a cache can’t open (a full disk, a permissions problem), the lookup returns a NullCache instead of raising, so requests carry on without that cache while the error is logged, and the registry tries again every 10 seconds until the real one is back. One call switches a cache off for a load test, and stats() gives an admin page every cache’s entries, size and errors.
from diskcache_oxide import Cache, Caches

# Rebuildable data: durable, so an outage is a miss, never an error page.
caches = Caches('/var/lib/my-app/cache', durable=True, timeout=1.0)
caches.register('pages', size_limit=2 * 2**30)
caches.register('api', size_limit=256 * 2**20)

html = caches['pages'].get('/about')  # opens on first use, the same object after that
caches.disable('pages')  # a load test without the page cache: no call site changes

for name, stat in caches.stats().items():  # for an admin page
    print(name, stat.count, stat.volume, stat.error)

# State (sessions, claims, queues) is a plain Cache, opened directly: a lost write must raise.
sessions = Cache('/var/lib/my-app/state/sessions', timeout=3.0, eviction_policy='none')
sessions.set('session:9f2c', {'user': 42}, expire=3600)

caches.close_all()  # at shutdown
sessions.close()
An entry is gone the moment it expires, for every read, len() and iteration. Its space is freed later: each set() clears a few expired entries, and nothing sweeps in the background yet, so run caches.expire_all() and sessions.expire() from a scheduled job about once an hour. Web workers shows where that job goes.
Talk Python runs its eight caches this way. Named caches covers the registry in full.
The example app is this setup in a whole FastAPI app, with gunicorn, a background worker and Docker Compose: a durable registry for pages, slow lookups and rate limits, and plain caches for sessions, job claims and a work queue. Every page shows which cache reads served it.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Where this is going
diskcache-oxide is being built in three stages. The first is done and the second is mostly done.

A better diskcache. The Cache and FanoutCache you already know, rebuilt in Rust: about half the read latency, many times the threaded throughput, safe across fork(), safe on free-threaded Python, and no pickle by default.
The complete local caching toolkit. Keys of every native type, memoize, tags, work queues, transact() and the coordination recipes (locks, semaphores, throttles, stampede protection) are all here. Still to come in this stage are a Django cache backend, free-threaded scaling, and a native AsyncCache for FastAPI, Litestar and friends.
A cache server. The same Rust engine served over the network: a Redis-style central cache for a fleet of machines, with SQLite underneath instead of RAM. As the only owner of its files, the server can use SQLite’s exclusive locking mode, which already measures about 40% faster reads than the shared-directory library.

See Vision and roadmap for how each stage breaks down.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Why diskcache-oxide

Fast where web apps spend their time. At a 99:1 read/write mix, one thread gets about 690,000 operations a second from a Cache, 1.6× diskcache’s rate and cheap enough to call straight from the event loop. Add threads and the gap opens: at 8 threads on a GIL build, diskcache’s per-thread connections pile into each other and its throughput falls to 19,000 a second, while oxide’s stays near 670,000, 35× ahead (the chart above).
Scales out across worker processes. A plain Cache has one write lock, so a server with a worker per core ends up queueing on it. FanoutCache spreads keys over several SQLite databases so writes to different keys stop waiting on each other. With 8 processes it runs 1.5 million operations a second, 5.7× a plain Cache and 1.2× diskcache’s FanoutCache, behind the same API and in one directory.
Built for free-threaded Python. The extension is compiled with gil_used = false and never leans on the GIL for correctness, which matters on a build where there’s no GIL to lean on. Every change is tested on 3.14, 3.14t, 3.15 and 3.15t.
Safe across fork(). gunicorn, Celery’s prefork pool and multiprocessing create workers by copying the parent, and the copy includes whatever SQLite lock a thread was holding at that instant. A process-wide fork barrier makes sure no child is ever born holding half a transaction.
No pickle on your disk. Values are msgpack (or JSON) with exact type tags, so tuples, sets, datetimes, dates, Decimals, big ints and NaN come back as what you stored, not as whatever the format could manage. Your own types are registered once and read back only where the name is registered. Pickle is opt-in, and a cache that didn’t opt in refuses to unpickle anything it finds, however it got there.
Predictable memory and disk. A bounded connection pool, a 1 MiB page cache per connection, a write-ahead log that trims itself back down, and a checkpoint() for when you want it empty now.
Correct under pressure. clear() never deletes writes that landed while it ran, a reader racing an overwrite gets the old value or the new one, never a spurious miss, and a queue never hands a worker another queue’s items or loses one it couldn’t read. Running the same test suite against both libraries turned up 19 bugs in diskcache, each with a reproduction in the repo. diskcache-oxide has none of them but one, which it keeps on purpose for compatibility (the list).
More than get and set. memoize caches a function’s results by its arguments. Tags group entries so evict(tag) removes a user’s or a page’s in one call. push and pull make a work queue every worker shares, handing each item to exactly one of them. Locks, semaphores and rate limits hold across every process on the machine, with no Redis.
A real off switch. NullCache turns caching off without a single if cache is not None: in your code, and can keep forwarding invalidations to the real cache while it’s off, so nothing stale is waiting when you turn it back on.
One place for all your caches. Caches is a registry for every cache in an app. Register each one once at startup, and code at any depth gets the cache it needs by name, caches['pages'], without passing cache objects down through constructors or a dependency-injection framework. Each cache opens on first use and every lookup after that returns the same object, cheap enough to do on every request.
Errors you can act on. Every exception says what went wrong, in words, and the errors page says what to do about it. Nothing is swallowed unless you turned on the setting that swallows it.
Typed. Ships py.typed and a CacheLike protocol that Cache, FanoutCache and NullCache all satisfy.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Status






Note



diskcache-oxide runs in production at Talk Python, Python Bytes and Talk Python Training. Every release runs three gauntlets first. A conformance suite runs the same tests against diskcache 5.6.3 itself, and every place the two differ is a deliberate decision, written down with its reason in Divergences. A sanitizer pass puts the whole codebase, bundled SQLite included, under Miri, ThreadSanitizer (with a free-threaded CPython built under it too), AddressSanitizer and LeakSanitizer. And a 24-hour soak throws processes, threads, forks, SIGKILL and clear() under load at one directory for a day, then checks it for corruption, lost writes and leaks.
Most of diskcache’s API is here: Cache and FanoutCache, keys of every native type, memoize, tags and evict(), transact(), the queue calls push, pull and peek, retry=, stats(), check(), eviction_policy='none', and the coordination recipes. Still to come: a Django cache backend, free-threaded scaling and AsyncCache. Deque and Index wait until someone asks for them, and reading a large value as a file (read=) is folded into a later large-file cache. Custom disk= classes and least-recently-used eviction aren’t coming; Vision and roadmap says why.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Install
uv pip install diskcache-oxide
It supports CPython 3.14 and 3.15, including the free-threaded builds (3.14t and 3.15t), on macOS, Linux and Windows. Wheels cover macOS on Apple Silicon, Linux (glibc) on x86_64 and aarch64, and Windows on x86_64 for all four Pythons, with the compiled engine and a bundled SQLite inside, so there’s nothing else to install. Anywhere else pip builds from source, which needs the latest stable Rust toolchain. Windows has no fork(), so the fork guarantees are Unix-only there; Getting started lists what else differs.
Before 1.0, a release that changes the on-disk format bumps the minor version and says so first in its changelog entry. Upgrading to one doesn’t break anything: a release that meets a cache in another format opens a new, empty one in a subdirectory named for its format (diskcache-oxide-format-3) and logs a warning, and remove_old_formats() cleans up the old one once the old workers are gone. A release that keeps the format keeps your caches warm. See Upgrading across a format change.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Coming from diskcache?
Change the import and point it at a new directory. That’s the migration. diskcache-oxide keeps diskcache’s API but uses its own file format (diskcache-oxide.sqlite), so it never reads or touches an existing cache.db:
# from diskcache import Cache
from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-oxide')
Switching from diskcache covers every difference you might notice, which is mostly things getting better and now and then things getting stricter.
